It seems to me that here is an example of a great initiative by a group of local people, some white, some Indian, working sometimes in concert with and at other times in opposition to the Department of Indian Affairs and the other do-gooder organizations that involve themselves in Indian affairs. They came up with a proposal which they submitted to the federal and provincial governments. I think the two governments are on trial. I do not think they have any choice but to go ahead and provide the money to this organization which has proven itself to be effective. It is completely independently controlled; it is autonomous; it is on its own. I think the minister should look into this matter as soon as possible with a view to approving the program.
I would like to say a word or two about the consultative process. Quite frankly, I have not been happy with the way it has been carried out, particularly with the way it has affected the Indian people of my area. The concept of the consultation process has been that the Indian, like the white man, is used to the operations of the white man's institutions.
1	think this is a false assumption. Basically, it has been my experience that there is no concept of representation, as we know it, on the Indian reserves. When I have consultations with the Indians, in the northern areas particularly, the chief will be telling me something and as he is speaking somebody, not a member of the band council necessarily, may interrupt him and make a correction or put

across another point of view. The chief will go back, reverse his stand, take that person's point of view into consideration, and go ahead. There is a sort of direct relationship here.
The consultation was imposed from the top down. The Indians were told to elect representatives and send them to the Lakehead or Toronto. They were taken out of their native areas and natural environment and put in a white man's situation. In this situation we expected them to provide us with proper information with regard to the Indians.
I admit that perhaps this is a little overdrawn, but I think the general idea is true. Far more work should have been carried out at the band level. There would have been far more understanding of the questions involved if this process had been carried out at the band level because the Indians would have known what matters were being raised. This is particularly true of Indians in rural and other areas where they are not in direct communication one with another. This was not done. To a large extent I think this was responsible for the first series of consultations not being as successful as we hoped they would be.
At this time I should single out the former minister of Indian Affairs, now the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Laing), for his initiative in setting up this program and for the work he did. If anybody could be said to be the father of consultations, it would be the present Minister of Public Works. Mind you, it was not a very pleasant form of consultation at times; sometimes it resembled a shouting match. Nevertheless, he believed in consultation and dialogue and went ahead and set it up.

Mr. Speaker, the debate thus far today has been conducted on a very high level indeed. As hon. members know, I am not one who usually becomes partisan in matters of this nature, and I do not intend to break that habit. To indicate the sincerity of that remark I will now do something that is usual and quite normal for me, that is, compliment a member of the treasury benches. I refer, of course, to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) who, in one aspect of his portfolio, namely, Indian Affairs, is making a very sincere effort to overcome an almost insurmountable problem, the tragedy of our Indian population. From time to time, of course, I will be critical of the other aspect of his portfolio, Northern Development, which is also my responsibility. In the meantime I believe he is making a commendable effort in regard to Indian Affairs and I hope that he continues along the present course.
I agree in large measure with what the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) said. He knows, as I do and as perhaps few hon. members who have not been in the northern area of our country do, the extent of the deplorable conditions which exist among our Indian people in that region of Canada. The minister has seen something of them and so have some of his officials, but not often enough.
One of the things on which I agree very positively with the hon. member for Skeena is his criticism of the department, more than of the minister, with respect to the administrative procedures now in force in connection

DEBATES	March 6, 1969
with the representations made from time to time by Members of Parliament. I happen to know of the procedure of which the hon. member for Skeena spoke according to which the problems are now handled by the Vancouver office instead of, as in my case, the Yukon agency or whatever agency handles the Skeena area. The problems mentioned in our correspondence are referred to Vancouver of all places. This procedure was invoked during the administration of the minister's predecessor and my belief is that it was done only for political purposes. There is no other logical explanation for it. This is very wrong. If the literally hundreds of representations which are made by Members of Parliament, in areas such as mine at any rate, on behalf of the Indian people require routing to Vancouver, then there is not much purpose in maintaining a Yukon agency.
As a matter of coincidence, before I even knew what was coming up in the house today I wrote to the minister's senior official in Vancouver and I sent the minister and the superintendent of the Yukon agency a copy of my letter in which I objected very strenuously to being obliged to go through this routine. The minister will receive that letter in due course. I wrote on behalf of an elderly Indian in my riding who was in need of assistance. My letter was dated February 4 and the reply from Vancouver was dated February 20. When there are people in need of assistance in weather 40, 50 or 60 degrees below zero and when the very matter of their survival is at stake, they cannot wait from February 4 to February 20 until these requests are funnelled through the usual channels before relief is obtained. So I urge the minister to consider the fact that no useful purpose is being served and, in fact, every evil purpose, by a continuation of that kind of nonsensical procedure. There is no reason in the world why the same procedure should not be followed that was in force for the ten and a half years prior to the imposition of the innovation of the minister's predecessor. There is no reason why the superintendent of the Yukon agency and his staff cannot handle these problems with which they can deal much more quickly than can Vancouver. I am sure the Vancouver office would be the first to agree.
This brings me to something else I want to say which I have not had the opportunity to do for some years now. It relates to the personnel of the department. I believe that the department has too few of the kind of dedicated personnel necessary to give any effect
March 6, 1969	COMMONS
to the purpose of the department. In the almost 20 years that I have been in the Yukon a consistently high calibre of field workers and personnel has been staffing the Yukon agency and dealing with the problems of the Indian people. It is too bad that I cannot say that giant steps in terms of progress have been made over the same period because despite the dedication of the personnel, despite their intention and their sincerity, they have been prohibited from achieving their desires and in some instances prosecuted for doing what was right. I am sure that if the minister consults his files and goes back in history he will know the people to whom I refer in making this comment.
It is very interesting to look at the proceedings of the Joint Committee of the House of Commons and the Senate on Indian Affairs in 1960 and 1961, starting at page 605 of the bound volume, and the recommendations that were set forth in the committee report of that day. They are almost precisely what we have been hearing on an annual basis ever since. It is little wonder that the actions or the lack of action of those responsible for improvement in the area of Indian Affairs can be described as they were by a northern Indian chief when he said: "Their words are like the snows. We learn to live with them but they always go away like their promises." I do not want to be critical of the minister and I hope he takes my remarks as being critical only of what is not being done.
I am in favour of the motion that has been put forward criticizing the government for its failure to deal adequately with Canada's native population. I believe that this motion must have the conscientious support of every member of the house because when the evidence is in one must conclude that the indictment is proven on all counts. The policies of the past several years and previous policies under all governments have simply not been adequate. I am reminded of the large amount of verbiage that has cluttered the pages of Hansard with respect to the Indian Claims Commission bill. I remember that the draft of that bill was first heard of in 1961 and I believe that in 1962 the bill was ready for parliament. However, along came an election that year. We have been hearing about the bill to establish the Indian Claims Commission every year since, but we do not have it yet.
The minister has asked for constructive criticism and I intend to relate my constructive criticism with respect to the department

Alleged Denial of Rights of Native Indians to my own riding, but I am sure that it applies equally to a good many others in Canada including the riding represented by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid). He said in his remarks that the Indian people of his riding are below the national average-I believe that was his description-and that it is only now that roads are being built into some of the areas where the Indian people live. In many communities in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories there are no roads at all and contact with the white people is infrequent, to say the least.

When one speaks of the Indian people one must think in the same breath, if I may coin a phrase, about the Eskimo population, and when I think of the Eskimo population I cannot but recall the words of Mary Carpenter, an Eskimo girl from Sachs Harbour, Victoria Island, Northwest Territories, 300 or 400 miles off the Mackenzie Delta, who is attending a university in western Canada where she is majoring in history and journalism. In a speech to delegates attending the national meeting of the Indian-Eskimo Association in Toronto last fall she criticized government bureaucrats for regarding the Eskimo as-and I am using her words now-a kind of new nigger in a parka, and for supporting the Panarctic oil scheme which exploits native lands. She told the delegates:
I don't wish to alarm you, but the fact is that the federal government is doing to my people what the whites have done to the negroes of the United States. They are making us into a service class people, or slaves; take your pick.
It is all very well to talk about the number of Indian children who are attending schools. It is all very well to talk in terms of statistics which are in themselves misleading. I made a note of the figures referred to by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. They look impressive, but what do they mean? What proportion of the increase of some 17,000 children of Indian lineage now attending elementary schools is the result of a natural increase in population? The statistics have to be related to that factor to mean anything at all. Again, it is all very fine to lay on educational programs for the Indian people, to produce more heavy duty equipment mechanics, more automotive mechanics, plumbers, electricians and so on. But training of this kind is of little use unless we can find ways of putting the newly trained tradesmen to work.
The minister has asked us for constructive criticism. I suggest it is of little use talking
6304	COMMONS
Alleged Denial of Rights of Native Indians about new policies, giving band councils more autonomy, sending more children to school and building more houses, if the department itself continues to create ghettos for Indian people as a consequence of the very things it is doing. This is precisely the situation in Whitehorse where what is literally a ghetto has been created. All the new houses for Indians built in the area are being constructed on land set aside for the Indian people- not on a reserve, because there are no reserves in the Yukon. Indians are not permitted to integrate with the other elements of our society in Whitehorse. Technically, I suppose, integration would be permitted, but it would cost money. Remember, it costs $4,000 or $5,000 to build a house on land set aside for Indians in the Whitehorse village. And I suppose it would cost between $12,000 and $15,000 to build any kind of home which would not reduce land and property values in the other residential areas of that community.
Look at the rest of the communities in the Yukon. Take Upper Liard, for instance. The chairman of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development, who is in his place today, knows that when the committee visited the Yukon recently the separation of the Indian community was immediately apparent to everyone. All these communities-Upper Liard, Teslin, Whitehorse, Car-cross, Haines Junction, Mayo, Burwash, Beaver Creek-are places where the Indian people are segregated. Homes are built for them somewhere out of town until, of course, the encroachment of progress demands more commercial land for industry or development and then the Indians are moved out again. Once this was done without consultation even.
The department would be well advised to get away from the idea that amenities for Indians have to be grouped in segregated pockets. If there is to be integration, instead of following a housing program in a ghetto let us build homes integrated with the rest of the community. If this costs more money, so be it; the end product will be much more useful to society than it is at the moment, and the present policy is not working anyway. In fact, it is a waste of money.
A few moments ago I mentioned the encroachment of progress. As things are at present, the right hand of the department does not know what the left is doing in the field of development. I think of the situation at Old Crow where there is an Indian population unique in all Canada, I suggest. We find there a community of ambitious, intelligent,

DEBATES	March 6, 1969
bright people who make their living primarily from trapping muskrat in a vast area known as Crow flats. Among us who live in the Yukon there is a great fear that the basis of their economy will be swept from beneath their feet as a result of the tremendous increase in investment interests in the oil and gas potential of this area as a result of the Prudhoe Bay discoveries. Great Plains Exploration has over 800,000 acres leased in this area. The side of the department concerned with development has informed the local press in response to inquiries that there are no oil and gas lands under lease within 200 miles of Old Crow. If extensive exploration is to be permitted in an unrestricted way in this area it will be the beginning of the end for these people because the economy of the whole region would be destroyed. The result would be another 250 people on welfare. I do not suggest to the minister that he place a tight cap on the development of our oil and gas resources anywhere in Canada, but I say there should be a very keen awareness of the possible effects of such development upon communities like Old Crow.
As my second constructive suggestion to the minister I want to say a word about the sad parade of humanity which one sees day after day, every day except Saturdays and Sundays, before the police magistrate or the justice of the peace primarily in the Northwest Territories. Anyone who attends these courts will hear charges being read to people who do not understand what is being said. Judicial personnel ask whether they understand the charges, and a nod of the head comes back in reply. "Do you plead guilty or not guilty?" they ask, and again a nod of the head is given, because if there is one thing an Indian person wants to do it is to please. Before he knows what has happened, let alone understands what has been read to him, he is convicted and fined $15 or $20. Because he has no money, he finds himself in jail for two or three weeks.

This government set up a commission in the Northwest Territories under Mr. Justice Morrow to study the situation. I suggest to the minister that the commission's recommendations apply to the Yukon territory as much as to territory lying on the other side of the Richardson Mountains. One recommendation was that Indian people ought to have a representative in court. It does not matter whether he comes from the Department of Indian Affairs or the Department of Justice.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I begin by saying that the minister had some good things to say today, especially when he announced that in future less paternalism would be displayed towards our Indian population since Indians are now able to speak for themselves. Frankly, some of us would take the minister's statements more seriously if we had not heard similar statements so often in the past. If my memory serves me correctly, the present minister is the fifth minister to hold the Indian Affairs portfolio since 1963. Former ministers were, I think, Mr. Favreau, Mr. Nicholson, the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Laing) and the minister responsible for regional development (Mr. Marchand). I may not be entirely accurate about the ministers who held the portfolio; yet, I think all this minister's predecessors made a speech almost exactly the same as the one he made today. The Indians of Canada will believe in the government's good intentions when they see actions taking the place of words.
I did not think I would ever agree with anything the premier of Saskatchewan said, but I must confess I agree with his assertion made in the provincial legislature in Regina yesterday that, with respect to our Indians, we are sitting on a time bomb. The St. Regis Indians have blockaded the bridge crossing their reservation. There is trouble at the Pas where the Indians have been picketing a health centre because they believe the person running it is displaying discriminatory attitudes. Then, we have the disgrace of Akaitcho Hall, Yellowknife, where the students are living under conditions that would not be tolerated by any other student group in this country. There, students 19, 20 and 21 years of age, are being treated as second class citizens. They are not allowed out in the evening without a written pass. They cannot go from the hospital to the gymnasium in the school
DEBATES	6305
Alleged Denial of Rights of Native Indians without obtaining a written pass and giving it back to their superiors when they return. They cannot smoke or drink, even where the law permits them to do so. In addition, they need a special permit to visit the old part of Yellowknife. Why is that, Mr. Speaker? Other Indians live in the old part of town, and the students need special permission before going there. The minister has had sufficient time to investigate what is going on in Akaitcho Hall. The difficulties there continue because many in this country believe that Indians are not as good as the rest of us. When the minister allows the current situation there to continue, he helps to foster the kind of thinking prevalent among some sections of our community. No wonder our Indians are concerned about what is happening.
I am ashamed that a magistrate of my city who sees Indians in court every day, and deals with their alleged infractions of the law, saw fit to appear on the national television program the "Public Eye" and make the statement reported in a letter that Chief Courchene sent. According to the letter, Magistrate Rice said;
I have never come across a married Indian Couple... There is something in their blood, I don't know what it is but an Indian and alcohol just don't mix ... An Indian woman told me-I guess she was an Indian, I can't tell the difference between an Indian and a Metis-if abortions were allowed she would have to have an abortion every morning.
In view of statements like these, is it any wonder our Indians are becoming restless, that they are beginning to demonstrate and that we face the possibility of violence? I suggest that the time for talk is over and the time for action has arrived.
The fifth annual review of the Economic Council shows that the life expectancy of the average Indian woman in Canada is 25 years, compared with 64 years for the rest of our population. Most Indians in Canada enjoy incomes of less than $3,000 a year and half our Indians enjoy incomes below $2,000 a year. Many Indians in this country live in poverty, and not much help is being extended to them. All these facts are well known.
Although it is important for us to know of the activities of the Indian Claims Commission, it is more important for us to know whether the government will act to help our Indians. Will it eliminate or reduce the bureaucracy which has directed every facet of Indian life here for more than 100 years? Will it allow Indians to decide what is good

6306	COMMONS DEBATES

The minister has been making all the right speeches. Although he insists that the reorganization of the department was only an internal, administration reorganization-I see he shakes his head in agreement-the Indians did not see it in that light. I have travelled extensively in this country and am aware of many Indian problems. I know Indian leaders in Manitoba, Alberta and in northwestern Ontario. Almost universally, they consider the reorganization of the department to be an attempt on the part of the bureaucracy within the department to grab more power.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
In the opinion of Indians with whom I have talked, the minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) is the pawn of the bureaucracy. They believe that the person who urged an extension of democracy for Indians and urged a policy whereby Indians would be given more and more say in deciding their destiny, was the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Andras). They believe that in the struggle for power which took place the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) opted for the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and for a further extension of this bureaucracy. Since those charges were made last October, the minister has repeatedly said they were not true. It really does not matter what the minister or I say, Mr. Speaker, because the time for talking is rapidly disappearing. In the next month or two the minister must cut down on the bureaucracy and give the Indians more say with regard to their educational problems, welfare and economic development matters. Unless the minister does this, Indians and other people in Canada will know that bureaucracy has won again, as it has for more than one hundred years.
There is no use in just talking, the minister must act. This is not the first attempt to permit Indians to have more say in their own affairs. It is only a matter of three or four years since the cabinet, on the recommendation of a minister who I think was the best that department ever had-

-the late Hon. Guy Favreau -approved a bold new program. I could read statements made by Mr. Favreau and other representatives of the government at that time regarding the program of community development whereby people trained in

social work, anthropology and social science would be employed by the department to live with the Indians and determine their needs. We were told this would be the salvation of the Indian people of Canada. Where is that community development program? It is gone. It is dead. The minister can say that is not true, but they went.
To demonstrate the truth of what I am saying, I want to quote from a letter written to the former Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson on January 4, 1968 by the then President of the Indian-Eskimo Association of Canada. I will quote a few paragraphs of that letter to prove the points I have been making. I read from this letter:
For more than a year, the concern of the Indian-Eskimo Association of Canada over the low attainment and apparent decline of the government's community development program in Indian reserve communities has continued to mount.
It goes on to say:
Our own assessment of the gross under-achievement of this program has been reinforced by repeated appeals from Indian persons and community development personnel in the field, both federal and provincial, urging the I.E.A. to seek a thoroughgoing appraisal of the program and its revitalization.
The letter goes on to say:
We take this course believing that the present program of community development is subsiding towards failure. While there may be many contributing causes, such as the costly failure to co-ordinate the scattered federal resources now being expended on community development, the program's real problems seem rooted in inappropriate administrative and management structures and methods and inadequate resources.
It later states:
Piecemeal measures or the pouring of additional funds into existing structures and programs will not, in our opinion, reverse or significantly change present trends. These trends lead to increasing dependence on welfare, high incidence of conflict with the law, low levels of economic capability and serious family and social breakdown.
It later goes on to say:
To bring the energy and intelligence of the Indian people into the struggle for standards of life equal to that of most other citizens will require a substantially new approach.
Then, Mr. Speaker, there are some recommendations in the letter:
In summary, we recommend:
That the principal developmental functions now housed in the Indian Affairs Branch be invested

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to make a few remarks in this debate about the native peoples. I should also like to commend the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) for introducing this motion. It is a good indication of the concern that all members of parliament have about the plight of the Indian peoples. I should say too that Canadians in all walks of life have never been more concerned about them. This is a good thing because, as has been generally known, the native peoples face some very great difficulties. The standard of living of too many of the Indian people in respect of income, health, housing, and other factors is much lower than is acceptable to the Canadian people. It would be useless, however, to dwell at
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Bechard),]
great length on all things that are wrong. I think many of the wrongs have been pointed out pretty adequately today by hon. members on both sides of the house.
The Minister of Indian Affairs, and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) gave an excellent address today. I think he presented a balanced picture of what the situation is today and what the government is trying to do to alleviate the conditions under which many of the Indian people are living. There are many, many good things the Indians are doing in addition to the many things that are wrong. I think the minister pointed this out as well in his remarks.
I should like to deal with a few of the remarks that were made today by some hon. members. The hon. member for Skeena referred to the problem as a fungus growth that is still growing and getting worse all the time, indicating that no progress has been made. I reject his suggestion that the Indian people are a fungus growth.

Then, why did you
not listen to what I said?
I did. I know the hon. member did not mean that some of us are fungi, but nevertheless the inference is there.
That is not true.

It is a
ridiculous statement and I reject it. The department is dealing with Indians. I think the hon. member should perhaps consider his choice of words. Under any circumstances, I reject the statement.

I rise on a matter of order, Mr. Speaker. I know the hon. gentleman wants to be truthful and correct. He is not being so in this instance. I do not want to become involved in a dialogue with him about it. What I said was that when, in 1867, the Fathers of Confederation decided that Indians on the land reserved for Indians should be under the exclusive jurisdiction of the federal parliament they started a program of paternalism. It is that paternalism that is the fungus growth which is still growing. I reject any implication on the part of the hon. member that I said otherwise.

I also reject the suggestion that we are not making any progress. Indians today are on the move as they have never been before. They are participating more and more in Canadian life
March 6, 1969

than they have ever done before. This is a good thing. We must participate as people in all aspects of Canadian life, economic, social and political. I should like to point out some examples of the progress the Indian people are making. These are not propaganda items from the Department of Indian affairs, as has been suggested by some hon. members. These are things the Indians are doing themselves. I have a clipping from the Financial Post dated August 10, 1968. The headline reads "Squamish Indians' enterprise transforms wasteland into profitable trailer park". The article goes on to say:
While some Indians across Canada are campaigning without much success for aboriginal land rights or seeking special concessions and compensation, Dan Baker, member of the council of the Squamish Indian tribe, has found that self-help and free enterprise can be far more satisfying-and profitable.
Dan, whose brother Simon is chief of the tribe, was inspired two years ago with what seemed at the time to be an almost impossible idea. The Squamish band for many years has held a strip of waterfront land facing Burrard Inlet, opposite Vancouver, some of which is now under lease to the municipalities of West Vancouver and North Vancouver.
At a point where the Capilano River, which rises in the North Shore mountains, meets tidewater near the Lions Gate bridge, there was a strip of timbered flat land undeveloped and apparently unwanted.
To Dan Baker the situation spelled opportunity. Wouldn't this be a wonderful location for a trailer park? The more he thought about it, the more he was impressed with the possibilities.
The land lies just across the Capilano River from the prestigious Park Royal area with its complex of high-rise apartments, shopping centres, specialty shops, theatres.
When Baker, with some encouragement from the federal Indian Affairs Department, made a modest start in clearing a part of the land for his trailer park, discriminating residents of West Vancouver, including members of the municipal council, were slightly aghast.
All that was several months ago. Today, it is obvious that Dan Baker's Capilano Mobile Park is an asset instead of any eyesore. Baker himself, his fellow tribe members and North Shore municipal officials are happy.
Because of the exacting standards set for intending residents-individual trailers cost from $8,000 to more than $20,000-the community has appealed only to people of means, many of them retired or semi-retired, who like the idea of living beside the river, in a dwelling free from the discomforts of apartment life and the inconvenience and high cost of maintaining conventional homes.

The land is leased by Baker and his partner, Roger Battryn, from the Capilano band on a three-year renewable permit, and the band receives 10 per cent of the gross revenue from the project, which represents a total investment of about $100,000.

In so far as education is concerned, more Indians are being educated than ever before, and more and more of them want to be educated. They want to be educated along with other Canadians, and this is being done.
I remember that when I went to university there were only three or four of us attending the University of British Columbia. That was in 1955. Today, Mr. Speaker, there are some sixty members of various Indian bands in British Columbia attending the University of British Columbia. I think this is progress. The hon. member for Skeena says that nothing is being done, that no progress is being made. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, the Indian people are on the move today as they have never been before.
I am not going to sing the praises of the government for its treatment of the Indian peoples. Successive governments have failed to do the job that was required of them. But I do not want always to dwell on the things that have been wrong in the past. We must address ourselves resolutely to the future.
I paid tribute in my maiden speech, Mr. Speaker, to the right hon. gentleman for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) for giving the Indians the vote. This was one of the great decisions that the right hon. gentleman made during his time as Prime Minister. I also said, Mr. Speaker, and I would like to repeat, that more was done for the Indian people by the government of the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson than was done at any other time in our history. I would like to just list a few of those things to refresh the memories of hon. members on the other side.
Mr. Pearson's government announced a $112 million housing program. Loans from C.M.H.C. were made available for Indians to build houses on the reserves. An off-reserve housing program was introduced. I spoke to many, many Indians about this in various parts of the country, especially in British Columbia where this program was welcomed and has helped them a great deal to find a new life in the cities where other Canadians are living.
Federal spending in the years 1962-63 on Indian affairs was about $51 million. Federal spending in the years 1968-69 is almost $140 million. I think this is progress. I think it indicates the government's concern about the

I agree with many hon. members who have said that the objective of all members must be to work for the minister of Indian affairs in order to see that he works himself out of a job. It is basically wrong that there should be a department of government devoted to a particular race of people.
I would welcome the abolition of the department of Indian affairs and the Indian Act. There should not be special status in Canada for any group of people. There should not have to be special laws saying that I am an Indian. We are all Canadians.
But, Mr. Speaker, I think it is unrealistic that we should expect the Indian Act to be abolished right now. This is not the wish of the Indian people. The impression that I get from them is that they would like to see progressive options made available in the Indian Act until they can get on their feet, do many things for themselves and function as communities on the same basis as many other communities.
The hon. member for Skeena talked about consultations and meeting the wishes of the Indian people. At another point he said that the government should abolish the department of Indian affairs. I am not sure what he means, Mr. Speaker, I do not understand this type of language. The minister of Indian Affairs made it pretty clear that we are consulting the Indian people as widely as possible on the changes that they want in the Indian Act. This is a good thing and I welcome it. Never before in history have such wide consultations been held to amend a portion of the Indian Act or the Indian Act in total. The Indian people have been very concerned that everything was coming from the top, being fed down to them and handed to them as a fait accompli. I am glad to say that this is no longer the case. I am confident that when the new policy on Indian Affairs is announced, the new act is introduced and the claims bill is introduced, the wishes of the Indian people will be reflected therein.
The hon. member for Skeena also quoted several figures in regard to average age at death, and in the same breath was talking about life expectancy. If the figures that the hon. member was using are true, I should be almost dead. I want to assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I think I still have a few years left.

clarify the record, average age at death reflects the age at which a certain number of persons die. Life expectancy reflects the average number of years of life for those who are still living. For example, if one person of 80 and a one year old baby die, the average age at death is about 40. If an 80 year old person and two one year old twins die, the average age at death is roughly 27. To clarify the record further, Mr. Speaker, the life expectancy of Indian men is 59.61 years at birth; life expectancy of non-Indian men at birth is 63.35 years. Life expectancy of Indian women at birth is 63.23 years; life expectancy of nonIndian women at birth is 74.17.

Statistics can often be misleading, and I am sorry to say that misleading statistics have often been used against the department of Indian affairs when it has been convenient for hon. members to suggest how bad things are. When the report on Indians and the law came out there was a story in one newspaper to the effect that 100 per cent of the women in the Kamloops jail were Indians. I was very alarmed at this statistic and I phoned Mr. Gus Godfriedson, an old friend in Kamloops, to ask what was going on and whether this was a true figure. He said, "Not that I am aware of. I know of one woman who has been in jail in Kamloops from time to time. If you call that 100 per cent, I guess the figure is correct."
With the best intentions in the world, members wound the Indian people when they use such figures. We are a proud people and there are many things that work against us. But most of them are not intentional, and we would hate to feel that they are.
As I have said before, the Indians have many accomplishments of which they can justly be proud. Most of us know that from time to time the department is a help. On the other hand, from time to time the department is not as helpful as we would like it to be. In our emotional moments many of us may blame the department for many things. But if we are to debate the future of the Indian people on an adequate basis, we will have to recognize that many things are being done by the Indian people. Many things are being done by various agencies of government, including the Indian Affairs branch. Still more things

Mr. Speaker,
I appreciate very much the statement of the hon. member who spoke before me, but nevertheless we much understand that within his party the hon. member may feel a little too bound to defend party policy. Certainly he is right to rejoice over the fact that we now appear willing to give a final solution to the Indian problem.

I would now like to make a comparison between the fate of as important a minority as the French Canadians and that of the Canadian Indians. We French Canadians have been fighting since 1760 against complete assimilation, against the loss of our rights and prerogatives. We are in a position to understand the problems of a race doomed to extinction, judging by the views which have been prevailing for a long time in this government.
So I can well understand the Indian problem. The principle according to which everyone should be allowed to remain himself is so true and enriching in a country like Canada that every effort should have been made in the past to make sure that the Indians, the first and most important inhabitants of our country, remain themselves.
The government is now trying to correct the situation and if the Indians themselves believe that this will be successful, I am the first to be delighted about it.
I doubt it, but this day may have helped in finding a real and definite solution to the problem.
I would also like to speak about the problems of the Eskimos, especially those living in northern Quebec. Even if it is now possible to give them the means to be independent, we should not prevent them from leading a fuller

So, if the Eskimos are ready to look after their own affairs, to invest their profits to their advantage in their own region, that could be a partial solution to the problem.
Consequently, foreign companies, and more particularly American companies, should not be allowed to take over the implementation of those contracts, to make profits and invest them in the States or in a country other than Canada, above all when Eskimos can run their business by themselves to their own profit. Apart from being an incentive for employment in those areas, the implementation of those contracts would enable the Eskimos to make money, as the Americans have always done. That would make them more independent, freer, for they would no longer have to make do with the welfare allowances that they get at the present time.
All those problems should therefore be considered in a very open way and we should not give with one hand what we take with the other. If we really want the Indians or the Eskimos to enrich our national heritage, we should let them have their own way and facilitate their self-determination, by all possible means.

He is one of the people in this house who took an interest in what has come to be called the Indian problem while numerous other Canadians, who at times now take a somewhat noisy interest in the matter, were quite silent and indifferent. If I start on a slightly critical note in reviewing what the hon. member for Skeena said, it is because I am leading up to a point. I should like to refer to one section of his remarks in which he was criticizing the booklet "Choosing a Path" which was distributed to the consultative groups as they met across Canada. The hon. member referred to the section which asked the Indians what they thought of the Indian liquor legislation. He went on to ask: Isn't this ridiculous? How many times have they been asked this question? Could they be blamed if they looked upon it as an insult to their intelligence?
Can we really say this, Mr. Speaker? It is true that they have been asked this question many times. It is true also that they have given many different answers. This does not apply only to Indians. The white people of Canada have, for many generations, asked this question about liquor control. They have given many different answers. They are continuing to give different answers.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
In my own province of British Columbia, the provincial government has recently set up another royal commission to investigate the problem of drinking in the province. So, I do not really think that it is an insult to the intelligence of Indians to ask them the question once again, or if it is, it is at least no more insulting than referring the question to yet another royal commission on behalf of the white community. I am not bringing this up to niggle on a small point but to lead to a point which I think is important, and it is this: There is disagreement among the white community in this nation on many issues, and there is disagreement among the Indian community on many issues. It is a good thing that there is. Occasionally, during the course of this debate I have heard mention of this figure called "the Indian" as though every Indian in Canada were somehow merged into a single recognizable entity. This mythical figure we call "the Indian" expresses the unanimous collective thoughts of all the Indians in Canada. This is a false premise and as

long as we persist in it in our handling of the important matters of Indian administration, administration by Indians themselves or by the Indian department, we cannot be right. There is no such man as "the Indian" in Canada. Indians are people of immense variety, and there is no reason why they should not disagree. It is true that, for instance, in most of the provinces of Canada there is a single Indian organization. Speaking in terms of fairly large organizations, there are at least four different Indian organizations in British Columbia which have slightly different views on what the course of their people should be. Occasionally these organizations are viewed somewhat critically by the white community. They say: "Why don't you people combine? Why can't you speak for British Columbian Indians with a single voice?"
Some of the people who ask this question sit in this house where there happen to be four political parties, not one of which is in total agreement with any other party. If it is right for us, then it is also right for the Indian, and this leads us a little further. It leads to the question of consultation with the Indians. Let us, and let the minister, recognize the fact that we cannot consult with the Indians of Canada and get one, single, cohesive answer as to what they want. In fact, it is almost an insult to suggest that we can go to the Indians from one side of this nation to the other asking: "Tell us what you want" and assuming that they are all going to tell us the same thing, therefore, it is merely a matter of meeting their requests in greater or lesser degree. This is not to happen. There are great variations even within a single area in my own riding of Coast-Chilcotin. I made a rough calculation a short time ago and I found that there were over 30 reserves in my riding. Many of the people cannot converse with one another except through the medium of the English language because their own languages are of such a vastly different nature.
In the course of the consultation meetings, how many points of view have been put forward on how the Indians feel as to their role as citizens of Canada, citizens of the province, citizens of North America and citizens of what might be called a pan-Indian society? In each case there are at least four distinct views held by the Indians. I should like to quote one from a publication called the "Indian Magazine" which I am sure many hon. members who are interested in this subject
March 6, 1969	COMMONS
receive. Let us see what Chief Max Gros-Louis of Huron Village near Quebec city had to say:
X can't see the Indians belonging to the provinces, because there's going to be another separation among Indians. We are already separated by the United States. Now if we start separating by provinces, that's going to be the end of the Indian.
That is one man's view. The consultative group has heard from Indians who positively want to be citizens of the province in which they reside. They feel that this is of prime importance to them. They feel that in many provinces of Canada they are being deprived, in greater or lesser degree, of basic rights as provincial citizens. There is a third view among Indians which is that the international border is an artificial line; that it is one which should not apply to them and that the Indian society is not of the nation of Canada nor of the nation of the United States but is a loosely connected society of a single group based on a single culture whose home is North America. There is yet a fourth view held that within Canada the Indian people are not Canadians but are allies of the British Crown; that they are a nation separate within Canada and that their true connection is to the Royal House of Britain.
I am not going to suggest which of these views predominates amongst Indians. I have some ideas, but I do not know whether it is up to me to suggest them at this time. However, I would point out that every one of these views has some legitimacy and every one of them has some followers in Canada. Therefore, whenever I hear that any man, particularly a white man but also an Indian, claims that he knows what all the Indian people of Canada really want, my faith in his knowledge and judgment is diminished. I bring this point forward in connection with the delays in bringing forth the new Indian act and the legislation for an Indian claims commission.
There is one difference between the present administration of the Indian department and those which preceded it. I think it is that we are attempting consultation with the Indian. As the hon. member for Skeena said, we have always claimed we were consulting them, but did we really do it? I can quote a good friend of mine in this regard, Chief Dan George of the Burrard No. 3 reserve. I recall him saying once: "Oh yes, the white man is always coming around and he says to us 'what do you want' but he never waits for us to answer".

There is one other point I should like to raise, and I feel it involves a moral responsibility on the part of the white majority in this country. There are many Indians who wish to leave the reserves, move into white society and integrate completely, losing their Indian identity. This should be their right. Since in most cases they are disadvantaged people, I believe we have a duty to give them special help in this regard. But what of the Indians who wish to remain Indians, who wish to live on their reserves and lead the traditional lives of their people? Is this not also their right? Do they not have the right, if they choose, to continue to exist as a separate, non-integrated group in Canadian society? It seems to me that both by treaty and in terms of ordinary justice the Indians who choose to remain Indians have the right to do so. Does this necessarily place them in the position of being second class citizens? I believe that throughout most of our history this has been the effect. By choosing to live on the reserves, by choosing to retain the old ways, they have tended to become second class citizens. Surely, the Canadian nation can find some way of guaranteeing that these people can live different lives without obliging them to be poor for the most part, as they are, or poorly educated, or discriminated against in any real way because they are Indians.
Surely, out of our present examination of the Indian Act the most important thing we can bring forward is a recognition on the part of the government, on the part of civil servants and on the part of the ordinary people

of Canada that when we meet an Indian we are meeting a person, one individual. And there is every bit as much variety among people of Indian ancestry as there is among people of any other race.
Before I close, I should like to comment on one point made by the hon. member for Skeena. I should like to give my fullest support to his plea for the early setting up of an Indian claims commission. Let us not fool ourselves. The government of this country has neglected to sign treaties such as the Jay Treaty and Treaties 8 and 11 in the north. We have made treaties and broken them. We have failed to make treaties in British Columbia west of the rockies, and in other parts of the north with the Eskimos. This record of doubtful faith, and in some cases of bad and broken faith, is a festering sore in this country. Let us not delay any longer than is necessary before forming an Indian claims commission to review these old disagreements, to patch up old difference and to start us in the 1970s with some of the old hatred and bitterness wiped away. I thank the house for its attention.
Hear, hear.

In the past several years, Mr. Speaker, certain changes have taken place in the attitude of Canadians toward the Indian population of this country. Public opinion has been aroused. It has been noticed, perhaps as a result of some publicity, that the Indian people are living in conditions which are not comparable with those experienced by non-Indian Canadians. There is an obvious disparity in their means of living in all aspects-a disparity in housing, in economic status, in opportunities for education, and in opportunities to seek the better things which this country has to offer.
As a result of this change in public opinion under the pressure which has been building during the past couple of years, the Indian affairs branch has decided to take a closer look at the Indian Act in its various aspects and to establish whether some of the difficulties which the Indian people experience today may not be correlated with certain aspects of this legislation. I think it is fair to say that public opinion has become aroused because our Indian population in general is becoming more educated. The more educated Indians have become outspoken and have brought their problems to the attention of the Canadian public.

This is a considerably better position than the bulk of the farmers who have surface rights only.

The most significant lesson I have learned is that in speaking of Indians we are not considering a homogeneous group, identically motivated and moving as one at the same pace toward universally shared objectives. It should not be surprising that they are as diverse in their capacities, their orientations and their objectives as any other similar sized sampling of people.

It seems to me that in this approach to Indians as a unit, the fallacy in our entire policy of the past lies. The fatal flaw of our Indian legislation since its inception has been this idea of considering Indians as a unit, rather than people the same as the rest of us. We are fundamentally wrong when we try, in a particular piece of legislation, to deal with all Indians as though they were a homogenous group, because we attempt to identify an average Indian to whom we can relate the legislation when there is really no such thing.
Having done that, we compound the felony, motivated I am sure, by compassion rather than colonialism, by reducing that average Indian to some sort of lowest common denominator to be sure that we do not treat any unjustly in a material sense, and in the process we treat almost all Indians unjustly in the spiritual sense.
The philosophical dilemma is far from new. I will refer here to the House of Commons debates in 1880, volume 2 at page 1990 and 1991. On the one side of the debate Mr. White of East Hastings said in part:
We are making them believe that the country will support them, and putting them in a position in which they have no credit or standing in the community. We should no longer treat the Indians as children. Something should be done to put them in a position to make them know and feel that they were responsible to themselves and to the country.
On the other side of the debate, Sir John A. Macdonald said:
You cannot make an agriculturalist of the Indian. All we can hope for is to wean them, by slow degrees, from their nomadic habits, which have almost become an instinct, and by slow degrees absorb them or settle them on the land. Meantime they must be fairly protected.
That was in 1880. Today, almost 90 years later, the same points of view exist.
The fact remains that Indians are now what is fashionably called, "a visible minority". Policies carried on by governments since the first Indian Act was enacted by the United Provinces of Canada in 1865 have made them basically welfare cases. Because they are a visible minority they are visible welfare cases. There is a stigma to that status, and whether or not we are or should still be obsessed by the guilt that was expressed in the debates of 1880, it seems we must now redirect the legislation and the policy behind it. We must abandon paternalism no matter how

Above all, we must orient our policy and the administration of it to individuals, to people, not to norms or averages, because when you deal with human beings there are really no norms or averages. The typical or average Indian is a fiction, a creation of administrative convenience. Continuation of the concept will invalidate any policy, however well conceived in its other dimensions.
I am heartened that even with the handicaps of the existing legislation the present minister and his department appear to have taken a human and a personal view towards the Indians, towards their responsibility. I have every confidence that in the new legislation coming before us as a result of the consultations that are going on today our policy for the Indians will be based on compassion and not paternalism, consultation not direction, and participation not dictation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I start by apologizing to any members on the other side whom I may have displaced in rising. May I also join many previous speakers in expressing appreciation at the high tone of the debate that has taken place today. This has been one of the more constructive debates it has been my pleasure to hear in this house. There have been 12 or 13 speakers in the debate this afternoon and this evening, every one of whom I believe has added something constructive to the review and to the considerations we must give in formulating a new policy. I do not think I can cover all of the highlights of the speech of each hon. member, but I will attempt to reply in general and to answer quickly one or two questions.
The immediately preceding speaker, known as "Weasel Horse", the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Gundlock), expressed concern at the delay in the national consultation meeting. In the interests of saving time, may I simply refer him to the remarks of my colleague the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) earlier today, and also assure the hon. member that we are giving consideration to the question of the number of representatives from Alberta. Some difficult problems are posed but we are going to be very open minded and do all we can to satisfy all concerned. I am sure that, with good will on all sides, a reasonable solution will be found.
The hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Mahoney), pointed out one rather agonizing section of the Indian Act which by itself, if for no other reason, indicates the great need for change. The hon. member referred to the Indian child who misses school occasionally
March 6. 198S
6320	COMMONS DEBATES
Alleged Denial of Rights of Native Indians and is automatically labelled a juvenile delinquent without due process of law.
The hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yew-chuk) had some worthwhile comments to make, though too many for me to refer to them all. He referred to the need for family planning. I was impressed by the way he put it, that we should ask the Indian people what they wanted, rather than in any sense imposing something upon them. He also referred to flying doctors. I think it is fairly well known that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) has been negotiating with the Canadian Medical Association and with regional and provincial medical associations to see whether a voluntary roster system could be instituted that would bring better service to Indian communities in more remote areas.
The hon. member for Coast Chilcotin (Mr. St. Pierre) made reference to the various differences of opinion existing among Indian people from coast to coast. I hope to refer to his rather interesting comments later.
The hon. member for Kamloops-Cariboo (Mr. Marchand) made a very pertinent observation when he talked of the need for all of us to recognize the great progress that is being made by many Indian people. So often in watching television I am concerned that, while undeniably poverty among the Indian people is shown, and while unfortunately there is a high rate of alcoholism and a rising rate of crime among the Indian people, a balanced picture is not presented. The other side of the coin, is not shown indicating the great progress that has been made by more and more of our Indian people. I think it is important that we give a balanced picture, and certainly that was one of the many contributions the hon. member made in his remarks.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) made several constructive suggestions with which I cannot deal in detail. One of them was the thought-a thought that we are considering-that there should be established Indian development corporations; that there is a general need for decentralization and for economic development as a whole. I also join with the hon. member in expressing my distaste of what I saw on the television program "The Public Eye" to which he referred, when a rather prominent citizen made such a bigoted comment about Indians, their blood content, and their difficulties with alcohol. I think this program made all of us

who are at all sensitive to the situation cringe.
The hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Simpson) and others referred to the need for a higher priority to be given by the government in meeting the problems of our native Indian people.
Hon. members will probably be surprised to hear me say that the motion that began this debate is a good one. I think the wording is appropriate and set the tone of the debate, which has stayed on a fairly high plane.
The corollary to this motion is for the government, I hope helped by the opposition, to not pursue a course, whether innocently, mistakenly or deliberately, that will meet the objectives and cause the results that are inherent in the words contained in the motion. We must, of course, remove and eliminate the destructive effects of paternalism by removing paternalism. We must eliminate discrimination, and discrimination there is in this country. In our course of action, we must restore human dignity, respect, pride and self-confidence to a group of people who have been alienated by many factors, not the least of which have been the policies of the past.
In his elaboration the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) went back-and this is what has impressed me most of all in this debate-to examine the basic assumptions upon which our policy should be founded. He questioned those basic assumptions in the comments or partial solutions that he offered.
Specifically the criticism that is inherent in the motion before us today is contained in an expression of cynicism as to whether the government is going to take action. All I would say about that is that personally I am absolutely convinced that it will not be very long before action is taken and that there will be a constructive change in policy. I appreciate the fact-and many people have made this point today-that it is no longer a time for sweet words and speeches; it is a time for action.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
The other inherent criticism in the motion, referred to by the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Simpson) and others, was the delay in announcing policy. I, and I know my colleague the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and other colleagues in the cabinet, are also impatient to take the necessary action and to move on this whole situation. When my colleague the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
March 6, 1969	COMMONS
and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) discussed with me the assignment to work with them in identifying the problems and to recommend to them and the cabinet possible avenues for change, I felt it was necessary to charge out because, in the first place, one of the more specific matters to accomplish was the immediate revision of the Indian Act.
The first meeting which I attended, in Yellowknife last July, taught me very quickly that perhaps speed was required but haste was not a good idea. There were many aspects of this whole situation that had to be examined in depth after consultation with and listening to the views of Indian people. I think the real point is that we must move on a timetable that is acceptable to the Indian people. We must not try to meet some artificial deadline that might be suggested, and in the process fail to apply the wisdom that the situation needs after 300 years of neglect and incorrect policies.
I think it would be presumptuous of us as a government if, after seven months of consultation with Indian people across this country and an exchange of views such as we had in the consultations ending only four or five weeks ago, we had presented immediately to this house, the Indian people and the nation a package policy. If we had done that, I think it would have indicated to all concerned that we had made up our minds long ahead of time and were not really listening to the recommendations and points of view expressed during the 17 consultation meetings just ended. We had to have time and we must continue to take the time, to digest all the views and opinions expressed in the last eight months. I cannot see the wisdom or value to anybody in proceeding with a new policy without the input that is necessary from all these consultation meetings.
There has been criticism of the consultation meetings. I think the degree of criticism is in many ways far from justified. These meetings were far from perfect, but we should not go to the other side of the spectrum and say they were hopeless, useless or, as some have said, a facade. They were open meetings. It may have been specifically said that the purpose of the consultation meetings was simply to examine the proposed revisions of the Indian Act. But from the very first meeting, and in every subsequent meeting, there was no attempt on anybody's part, whether he was a minister or not, to suppress any point of view expressed about any matter bothering the Indian delegates who attended.
DEBATES	6321
Alleged Denial of Rights of Native Indians
These meetings covered the whole range of local problems, regional problems, national problems, the Indian's suspicion of government, their cynicism, treaty rights' and aboriginal rights; in fact, the whole gamut and range of frustrations and grievances that has built up over the centuries in respect of the non-Indian, Indian relationship. So, there was no suppression. Although these meetings may not have reached all the objectives we might have had in mind, I think it was a very valuable exercise and within a short time there will be in the policies that will be announced some indication of the value that came from those meetings.
As most hon. members know, there were 17 meetings. I believe all but one of them was attended by a minister, either my colleague the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development or myself. Of the 17 meetings I know my colleague was at eight, and I was at ten. There was only one, in Prince George, which we regret we did not attend. This was due to circumstances which arose very suddenly and could not be avoided.
There are in this country 558 Indian bands, and in those 17 consultation meetings 530 were represented. I think that is a pretty good representation. This brings to mind one of the problems we face and with which we must deal. We must have understanding in this respect, and perhaps some adjustment from the Indian people themselves. The hon. member for Kcnora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid) referred to the fact that Indian people do not view representation, the delegation of authority and the appointment of spokesmen, in the same manner as non-Indians. I have learned during the last few months that there is a tendency in the Indian community to seek consensus and unanimity. Often no one person is designated as the spokesman for a group of people. Often at these consultation meetings an Indian delegate would rise right at the beginning, to make it clear, and say: I speak for myself. In their gentle, effusive and humble way they would indicate that they were not taking unto themselves the authority to speak on behalf of other people.
There were many things wrong with the consultation meetings. There was insufficient opportunity for the Indians to consult amongst themselves beforehand, I think we have learned a great deal from that. At the same time, I think it was an exercise in consultation the like of which has never before been conducted by any government with any group of people in this country.
March 6, 1969
6322	COMMONS
Alleged Denial of Rights of Native Indians
We are embarking upon new policies. New policies will succeed, obviously, only if we insist in seeking the right answers with clarity and consistency in both the definition of the objectives we are seeking and the selection of the means of realizing them. In this process we must all ask ourselves certain basic, fundamental questions. Then, we have to try and answer those questions. Hopefully, from the questions and the answers will come enlightened policy. Some of these questions are: In what way are Indians excluded from our society? In what ways have they been disadvantaged? How did they come to be that way? What obstacles stand in the way of their achieving equal citizenship and full participation? Then the obvious question is: What actions and measures can be expected to overcome these obstacles?
I think in answering these questions it is important to examine the jurisdictional, legal, administrative, social and economic factors which shape the present status of Indian people and native peoples in our society. We must look at the special legal status of these people. We must recognize and consider the poverty aspects involved, their alienation, cynicism, mistrust of government and obvious isolation from the larger society.
The hon. member for Skeena referred this afternoon to the supposed basis for federal government acceptance of responsibility in this field. He referred to section 91, paragraph 24, of the British North America Act, which assigns the making of laws, of legislation respecting "Indians and lands reserved for the Indians" to the jurisdiction of the federal government. I do not know that this, to the exclusion of change, means that it has to be totally, utterly and exclusively the responsibility of the federal government and under its jurisdiction.
Anyway, on that assumption many years ago, and as a consequence, the Indian Act was passed, an administrative structure was created and special policies were developed for this particular ethnic group. Further, the federal government became involved in the provision of a complex set of services for Indians which other Canadians receive from provincial and local governments.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
The basic source for defining the policy of the federal government has been the Indian Act. As hon. members know, it is a comprehensive act which defines who shall be considered an Indian and how one can give up
[Mr. Andras.l

Indian status. In so doing, it establishes a special legal category defining certain rights and imposing certain restrictions. It contains provisions1 dealing with the reserve system, a system of local government, and special sections relating to taxation, liquor, inheritance and education. Although the federal administrative structure, the department of Indian affairs, stems from the Indian Act, a growing number of important departmental programs are marginal or peripheral to the Indian Act: welfare, health, community development, economic development, manpower programs etc.
This has been referred to before as well today, and I will bring it up again. The fact is that the treaties signed with Indians add another dimension to Indian-government relations. Almost all Indians express strong resentment at the failure of the government to honour and fulfill treaty and other obligations and promises. The most important of these pertain to hunting, fishing and trapping, and to the provision of land.
Hon. members have made reference today to the fact that most social and economic indicators show that the majority of Indians live in sub-marginal conditions and that relative to the rest of the population the gap in income levels, health care, educational achievements and occupational skills, while improving, is actually growing wider between the Indians and the non-Indian society. There is a significant factor explaining poverty among native peoples in Indian communities, and that is their geographical dispersion and, in many cases, the remoteness of native communities. In addition, their limited mobility has contributed to making employment and participation in the economy difficult. As a consequence, Indians have been isolated and excluded from the larger society, and the exercise of their basic human rights is seriously restricted.
We have to recognize also that cultural barriers and the insensitivity of the non-Indian society to the heritage and values of Indian life have played and continue to play a major role in excluding native peoples from the mainstream of Canadian life.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, through you I would like to thank the hon. members for their courtesy in letting me go over my time. I was wound up, and I had no idea the clock was moving that quickly.
I was commenting on the fact that I think we also have to take into consideration, in the evolution of the new policy, the fact that there is an insensitivity of the non-Indian society to the values of Indian life and that this has been a factor in excluding Indians from the mainstream. These barriers are most easily observed at two crucial points. If they could be overcome we could go a long way to correcting the situation.
These two points are where Indians come into contact with our industrial society, in educational institutions and in the labour market. Many native students enter the school system with obviously different cultural orientations and often limited or no knowledge of English or French. The educational process, one of the major instruments of socialization in any society, proves to be for the majority of Indians a maladaptive experience. In terms of getting a job, in many ways the traditional Indian way of life has not prepared the individual for occupational roles in the Canadian labour market. The new demands that they have to face-and so often they face them with a lack of understanding on the part of the people with whom they are mixing-are hard to adapt to and frequently force the Indian person into accepting sporadic, low skill employment instead of a career oriented occupational role.
Alleged Denial of Rights of Native Indians
I believe, and I know my colleague joins me, that in the past Indians have not been adequately consulted nor has their point of view been sufficiently considered in the formulation of policy and the application of programs affecting their lives. Regardless of the type of program, such paternalism and noninvolvement only encourages apathy and reduces the effectiveness of any measure because there is a resulting lack of acceptance.
This is a brief expose of the tangled web of jurisdictions, constitutional problems and contradictory objectives. That web must be untangled. I doubt there is any one single group of actions that will provide instant solutions to the deep social problem that we face with regard to our native people. However, one fact is clear. There must be change, and change there will be. Again I congratulate the hon. member for Skeena and I agree with him that in order to provide meaningful change we must go back to the basic assumptions.
The alternatives'-and I just throw these out without commitment because, as hon. members know, we are not in a position to delineate or define our policy-will obviously range from a tremendous increase in the existing structure with more budget applied to it and more people to do more of those kind of things on the one hand, to an alternative similar to the one implied by the hon. member for Skeena, or perhaps some alternatives in between these two. But whatever decision is made as to the basic objective, we must be very careful in analysing, and seeing with all the wisdom that we possess, the consequences that will flow once we have identified the objective we want to pursue. Whatever that solution will be, it must take into account the fact of the poverty among the Indian people. It must given consideration to treaties and rights and the views and attitudes of Indians toward treaties and rights. It must take into consideration and counteract the deeply rooted alienation that exists among the Indian people.
The other point which we must take into account and which has been mentioned by many hon. members is that because of the diversity of opinions and diversity of problems-which incidentally are similar to those found in almost any comparable sized group in Canada, whatever their origin or their racial background-we must be very flexible in our solutions. I do not think we can have one single approach to this.
