that some of the people objected to it being held at this time, that they wanted it held over so they could examine what had been presented, and so on.
The native Indian people are also concerned about the Indian Claims Commission bill, and I should like to tie that into my remarks at this point. They consider that there is an element of deceit and falsehood on the part of the government. Last October the government put on the order paper a notice indicating it was going to introduce the Indian Claims Commission bill; I forget the exact date of the notice. Having been questioned about the Indian Claims Commission bill, the minister rose in the house and said he had taken the bill back. It had been hidden to start with. It was not given to the people at the consultation conferences. In any event, the bill was taken back for revision as a result of some of the views expressed and representations made at the consultation conferences.
Withdrawing the bill is fine, but it was accidental. Nobody at the consultation conferences had seen the Indian Claims Commission bill. They did not know what was in the government's mind but they accidentally hit upon some of the weaknesses in it. I should like to know how many more weaknesses are in the bill. Today the consultation conference in Ottawa was supposed to meet and we have not seen the bill yet. The minister shakes his head. Did the minister delay the conference because the bill was faulty? The minister indicates no. When is the bill going to be ready? The minister says soon.
My mother had a saying about "soon" which was related to a cat that we had. She called the cat a "sooner". It would sooner stay inside and perform the natural functions than go outside on a cold day. Soon does not mean anything, and I am sure the minister would not want to be classified as a sooner. The native Indian people want to know where the blazes this bill is. Is the minister having trouble getting it through cabinet, or with his associate minister? Does the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) not agree with what has been presented in the bill? These are serious questions to which our native people want an answer.
I have talked with some of the people who were delegates to the conference that was supposed to have been held today. Two of them told me they may not even bother to come when it is held because they are so fed up with all the delay and procrastination.
Alleged Denial of Rights of Native Indians They have seen what has gone on at the consultation conferences and want no further involvement.
I was going to make some mention of housing which is a pretty serious problem for our native Indian people. One of the communities in my constituency has 30 families on a priority list waiting for houses. If you go to practically any Indian village in Canada you will find two or three families living in the same house. In fact, the word "house" is a euphemism. You see six or seven little kiddies sleeping in the same bed, and the same thing in another bedroom. People have to sleep on couches in the living room. Students are unable to do any meaningful homework in that sort of environment because conditions are overcrowded and youngsters are wandering around, as well as grandparents and parents. Too many people are living in the same house. Where is the quality of life here?
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
All these people are living in the same home for two reasons. The first is that the average income a few years ago was $1,600 per family. The second is that the government, through its departmental administrative structure, spends twice that much money per family which does not filter down to the people. Another problem is that these people do not have the opportunity to become meaningfully employed, to do some work and earn an income, because the government has failed miserably in its attempts to develop anything worth while in terms of job opportunities and economics.
The government says it is helping with its housing program and building homes for these people. Do you know, Mr. Speaker, what kind of homes are being built for elderly citizens, some of whom have to live by themselves in two-room shacks? These elderly people have difficulty getting around at the best of times, but the houses for them are built without inside toilets or running water. These people have to take a bucket and walk outside to the seashore because they do not have a sewer system or the amenities of life that we believe standard in our society. This is disgraceful.
The propaganda machine in the department grinds out propaganda about the houses being built and the money being spent on this program, etc., etc. But this money does not reach the individual human beings who live in this sort of environment. It is no wonder that
March 6, 1969
6290	COMMONS
Alleged Denial of Rights of Native Indians Ross Thatcher, the Premier of Saskatchewan, is reported to have said yesterday that a time bomb is ticking. That time bomb has been ticking for the last four or five years and its tick is getting stronger and stronger. So far neither I nor many native Indian people have seen any indication on the part of the government that it intends to do anything meaningful or worth while to cope with particular problems such as this.
The younger people are simply not content to go through the same sort of degrading and denigrating situation that their parents went through. They are no longer content to live in these places called reserves but which are nothing more than isolated economic concentration camps where there is no opportunity to realize the full benefits of our society. They are fed up with being treated and looked upon as a group apart from the rest of society. The hon. member for Kamloops-Cariboo (Mr. Marchand) will tell the government this, as he undoubtedly has. Ask any person of native Indian origin, and he will tell you the same thing. He is not interested in having his problems dealt with from the point of view of his cultural background. There is within the concept of our social order and within the concept of the department too much looking upon this situation as an "Indian problem". I put the words "Indian problem" in quotation marks. It is not an Indian problem; it is a social problem that confronts native Indian people to a far stronger degree than it does anybody else.
Native Indian people are underprivileged Canadians, far more so than any other single ethnic group in this nation. Their problems have to be coped with on that basis, as problems confronting people, problems confronting human beings. We have to develop within the department, within the government structure, something more than has been developed before. The government has to head in the direction of getting out of the business of interfering in other people's lives. It must provide them with the opportunity to realize those values of human dignity and quality of life that promote self-respect and enable the individual to have a feeling of pride and respect for himself as a human being. The native Indian has not had this opportunity up to now.
The government must embark upon a program which will provide people with opportunities to develop human freedoms, economic freedom, economic opportunity, work and


not welfare. Only in this way can the native Indian have the advantage of the amenities of life and the services of our society. Only in this way can they appreciate these things and be on an equal basis with other Canadians.
The government has to deal with the human, fundamental rights of people on the basis that they are Canadians first and that the native Indian is confronted with social problems more serious than those of other people. There have been 100 years of repression and suppression of the rights and freedoms of the native Indian people. This fact must be counterbalanced in the shortest possible period of time. A century of wrongdoing will take a little while to undo. It has to be done by deliberate and conscious effort. It cannot be done by pious hopes or propaganda; it has to be done by accomplishment. The accomplishment has to be related to a period of time when there will no longer be a person at the head of a department that is set up to deal with the problems of people on an ethnic or cultural basis. That is discriminatory, wrong, and terribly shocking for people to have to accept. The minister should know this better than anybody.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58 (11)-ALLEGED DENIAL OF FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS TO NATIVE INDIAN PEOPLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great attention to the speech of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard). I thank him for the reasonable tone in which he made the speech. The hon. member raised many of the fundamental questions that I, as Minister of Indian Affairs, have in mind. I thank him very sincerely for taking this approach to the problem.

Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that we inherited years ago the problem facing us today with regard to the Indian people in Canada. The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) claims that during the last century we built, within our own society, a separate group which is known as the Indians of Canada. Because of their ethnic origin and the colour of their skin, they are governed by a group of institutions other than those set up for the other Canadians citizens. This is a serious problem which the government is now looking into carefully.
In the last few months, we have had a series of consultations with the Indians of Canada. We have held 18 meetings across Canada and I am pleased to report to the house that we attended these consultations primarily to listen to the Indians.
March 6. 1969	COMMONS
It is true that we had given them in recent months a booklet entitled Choosing a Path outlining certain points to guide their discussion.
But when my colleague, the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Ondras) and myself participated in those consultations, we discussed all the matters the Indians brought up. We listened to them and never did we try to impose our views upon them.

It is very clear at this moment that at these consultations the message of the Indians was loud and clear. They do not need any lawyers; they do not need anyone to speak for them. They have shown the people of Canada that they can speak for themselves. They spoke about their problems. It is very clear that they want to be full citizens of Canada; they want to share both the advantages and responsibilities of being Canadians.
I think we have understood them. They have spoken about their treaty rights and aboriginal rights. We have listened to them and will respond to them. They want more autonomy. They want to make decisions, at the band level, for themselves and by themselves. We have understood them, and when we come up with our new Indian policy they will see that we have understood that message.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
I think we made a lot of progress over the last seven months in our consultations and our dealings with the Indians. For the first time we have provided them with a genuine opportunity to talk to the people of Canada. It is being said that there are too many civil servants around, but you cannot operate a government department without having civil servants to do the job. One of the factors to be considered is that the way in which we have organized these consultations has provided the Indians with the occasion to speak not only amongst themselves but to the people of Canada.
The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) blamed us for having spent some money on public relations. It is true that we did so at these consultations but it was done with the purpose of providing the Indians with the opportunity to speak to the people of Canada. At these consultations we made sure that the press and television cameras were there. I will not apologize to anyone for having provided the Indians with that opportunity, and I
DEBATES	6291
Alleged Denial of Rights of Native Indians think that these consultations have been profitable.
It is true that I have postponed the meeting we were supposed to have today. The reason is that the consultation was to terminate at the end of December but at the request of the hon. member for Skeena and of his constituents we held another meeting at the end of January in the riding of Skeena to listen once more to the Indians in that riding. I was there and so was the hon. member. I said almost nothing and the hon. member said nothing at all; all we did was to listen to the Indians. Their message was loud and clear.
We have put every word the Indians said on tape and it has been transcribed. All this takes time. We have not yet sent the report to all the delegates, and it would have been unfair to the people of Skeena to call them to Ottawa today when their views were not yet made known to the other Indians of Canada. I postponed the meeting because some of the Indians who want to come here and have a meaningful discussion with the authorities want to have more time to study the views of Indians from other parts of Canada.
The hon. member has accused us of not being ready with the Indian Claims Commission bill. There are many reasons for that. I gave a reason in December-because further representations were made at the consultations. I said that perhaps I will have to take another look at the bill. The hon. member for Skeena disappoints me because for months and years he has been speaking about the situation of Indians in Canada. I realize today that he is beginning to be out of touch with the people in his own riding.
The president of the Nishga tribal council, who is a member of the New Democratic Party and an Indian, Mr. Frank Calder called me to urge me not to proceed right away with the Indian Claims Commission bill because their case is before the court in British Columbia and they do not want it to be prejudiced. He is an M.L.A. out there and he asked the hon. member for Skeena to ask me to postpone the bill because they do not want me to jeopardize their case before the B.C. court. That is one of the reasons why we have not proceeded with it.
I am not too shy to respond to a reasonable request by the very Indians who perhaps in part vote for the hon. member for Skeena. Right now we are engaged in reviewing these consultations. We are studying them because we want to come up some time in the future-the hon. member for Skeena does not
March 6, 1969
6292	COMMONS DEBATES
Alleged Denial of Rights of Native Indians want me to use the word "soon"-with a positive policy which the hon. member will look at favourably because we think we will change many of the rules.
I have said many times in the house that it is true that the present Indian Act is too paternalistic. Out of the 135 clauses in the act there are 111 where it is said that the minister has to do this or that or should do this or that. I have spent hours in my office signing documents which permit Indians to borrow $3,000 or $4,000 from the C.M.H.C. I am ashamed at my age to appear to be the white father of the Indian population. I think we have to change many things but we cannot do this before completing the first round of consultations. The hon. member blames us for doing things without consulting the Indians and yet although we have not completed the consultations he rises in the house today to blame me for not proceeding with the claims commission bill. I hope that next month, although I cannot give a specific date today, I will be able to listen to the views of the representatives who have been chosen by the Indians. Following this I will come to the House of Commons and tell the members what the government plans to do to solve the problems of the Indian people of Canada.
I made speeches in which I said that one of the problems in Canada is that the provincial governments do not consider Indians to be citizens of the province. I say that Indians should be citizens of the province equal to any one of us because they are human beings like any one of us. The government is ready to try to find a solution to this difference in views.
As the hon. member said, we cannot solve all these problems overnight but there are some fundamental questions to which we must reply. I can assure the house that as soon as the consultations with the Indians are over the government will make up its mind on the new Indian policy to be adopted and will inform the house of it.

Mr. Speaker, during the election campaign we spoke repeatedly of the Indian problem. And the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) himself mentions it in all his speeches, on the rights of the citizens.
This government is extremely concerned with it, and that is why we have given it a priority it did not have before.
I could speak of what we have done in the past. We are accused of having spent too

much money on the Indians, of having increased the budget too rapidly in the last few years. It is true that we have spent a lot of money; still, one must be objective. We have more than tripled our expenditures for Indian affairs in the last few years, that is from 1962 to 1969, and we have produced some results. We may not have built enough houses, but we did build approximately 10,000 units since 1963. We have given better schooling to the Indians. Ten years ago, only 15 per cent of Indian children stayed in school after the 5th grade. Today, 95 per cent of the school age children in the Indian population of Canada have gone beyond the fifth grade.
We said that we wanted to give the Indians more autonomy. We have taken the necessary steps towards that end. For instance, Mr. Speaker, we have had discussions with the Manitoba Indians for this very purpose. As they are organized and as they have expressed the wish to administer their own affairs, we are ready to negotiate with them and with the provincial authorities towards an agreement giving them the opportunity to assume a greater share of the responsibilities.
After having criticized us freely, the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) will perhaps allow me to read the comments of the person who surely knows quite a bit about the problems of the Manitoba Indians, and I refer to Mr. David Courchene.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)

Mr. David Courchene said:
-the meeting is possibly the biggest step forward in Indian-white relationships.
He attributed the new approach to Indian affairs to the valid demands of the Indians and a new federal minister of Indian Affairs who understands the problems the native people face.
We have really created a meaningful partnership with the government.
As I said previously, I do not feel very much at ease with a situation in which we have to decide every step of the lives of the Indians. They have now found spokesmen among themselves and on most occasions they express their views very well. And we have been listening to them. We have to give more authority to the Indians at the band level in order that they may decide their own priorities. We have to permit Indians to gain access to the same institutions as do other Canadians. Recently a measure was passed in this house, though little has been said about it,
March 6, 1969	COMMONS
giving Indian farmers the opportunity to borrow money from the same institutions as do white farmers. Because of the very nature of life on a reserve the Indian population often has no access to the same institutions as do their competitors.
We must develop new policies and new programs to permit Indians to enjoy these facilities. I cannot be specific today, for the reason that we have not yet completed our consultations with Indians. But we have understood what they have to say and we shall follow through with the necessary measures once we have completed these talks. I think we shall make them full citizens of Canada, because they want to be full citizens. We will give them more autonomy because they want more autonomy. In many instances they are able to conduct their own affairs. However, we ought to be objective about this question at all times. We should not be too partisan in the face of one of the most difficult social problems of our time. I am glad this debate is taking place today because it will focus the attention of the House of Commons on this question. I do not want to speak for too long because I know I shall be coming right back here with new policies on Indian Affairs after the consultation process has been completed.
The hon. member for Skeena would like me to drive myself out of a job. I would not mind that very much. I can probably do something other than Indian Affairs; at least I can look after the other part of my department. As I say, we should not be partisan about this. I think the hon. member for Skeena is to be complimented for keeping the level of the discussion so high.
We know there are many problems to be solved in the fields of housing and employment for Indians. We should not be helping these people because they are Indians but rather because they are poor or because they lack sufficient education. It is a kind of discrimination when one recognizes, within a society, a group because of its colour. I think we should deal with this issue because it is a social problem, because these people need more education, better housing accommodation, better economic opportunities, and so on.
We have really done a great deal in this direction during the past seven months. We have helped the Indians of Canada to form their own Indian association. They have held meetings in Ottawa. We have invited them here, we have paid their expenses, we have
DEBATES	6293
Alleged Denial of Rights of Native Indians provided them with opportunities to talk with me, with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and with the officials of the department. They were in Ottawa for a week during December during which we helped them form the association. Since then we have made sure that the National Indian Brotherhood was represented whenever we held consultations. I think we have achieved a lot in the way of co-operation with the Indian Brotherhood.
Unfortunately, I cannot tell the house today what the new Indian program is to be. We have been obliged to postpone some of the things I was very anxious to do because I felt it was my duty to listen to the requests of the Indians themselves. We should not rush forward when they are not ready. The consultations we were to have held today have been postponed at the request of the Indians themselves and because we have extended the first round of consultations following special representations by the Indians of Ontario and of the Skeena riding.
I do not wish to take up much time today. I merely want to say it is somewhat unfair to suggest we have made no progress in relations with our Indian population. The emergence of the Indians will come about from within themselves. There are some within this community who can show that we have made a lot of progress in many fields. Our role is not to be paternalistic toward them, though we could be paternalistic in many ways. Sometimes we can be more paternalistic in agitation than we can be in administration. We must be very careful not to make this a political balloon. We ought to make sure that the Indians have the opportunity to express themselves and solve their own problems. In the new policy formed pursuant to the present consultations we shall show we have decided to agree that they should be full citizens of Canada and give them access to the same institutions as are available to other Canadians.
I am sure many hon. members would like to express their own views on this subject today. I welcome positive suggestions and I should like hon. members to put forward their ideas as to possible new programs and approaches so as to help us bring in the policy we shall soon be announcing, making the Indians of Canada equal to any other citizens in our country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58 (11)-ALLEGED DENIAL OF FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS TO NATIVE INDIAN PEOPLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate which the house is conducting today is certainly most timely. In fact, it is long overdue. As the hon. member for Skeena
March 6. 1969
6294	COMMONS
Alleged Denial of Rights of Native Indians (Mr. Howard) said, it is a considerable time since the house has had an opportunity to discuss this important subject, and I do not doubt that all hon. members will realize that it is, indeed, an important subject. I say this because should we, as legislators or as Canadians, fail to attack this problem in a meaningful way and do our best to enable our Indian people to become equal partners in society, it will be increasingly hard for future generations to do so.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
The hon. member for Skeena spoke of those subjects which concern our Indian peoples today. He spoke of the necessity of maintaining human dignity, cultural identity, and the desire of the Indians to take their full part in Canadian society. I was pleased to hear the minister say the government was anxious to attack these problems as quickly as possible. I notice he said that the government had inherited its problems. That is quite right. Similar problems have faced other governments. It is gratifying to find that Canadians now think present difficulties in this field should be cured quickly.
I was pleased to hear the minister say that there had been consultations where representatives of the government met representatives of our Indian peoples. It will be agreed, I think, that members of all parties have insisted on such consultation over the years. When one speaks of consultation one must ask, to what extent is it being carried on? One must remember that when governments plan new legislation affecting our Indian peoples much time is spent by so-called experts and legal advisers in preparing and planning it. Such planning can go on for many months. After all that work the minister and some of his officials may go to the Indian people, outline the proposed program in one or two brief meetings and expect the Indians to digest the program and say which parts are acceptable and which are not. We speak of consultation, and we must remember that our Indian people need time and all the assistance we can give them if they are to examine plans that the government proposes in an adequate manner.
The present attitude of the government which has led to consultations being held with the Indian people is a far cry from the attitude that prevailed not too many mears ago. Hon. members will no doubt recall that the actions of Liberal ministers were severely criticized when health services to our native


peoples were to be cut back. Without prior notice being given to the heads of our Indian communities, regional directors of health services were informed that health services to Indian peoples would be curtailed. Hon. members of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition and members of other opposition parties took great exception at that time to what was happening. It is therefore gratifying to see that the government has now adopted a different attitude and is willing to consult our Indian peoples before presenting legislation to the house.
The hon. member for Skeena said that the minister should be working toward the abolition of his department and portfolio. I am sure the minister realizes the hon. member was not being critical but was expressing a hope. He was trying to say that not only the minister but all officials of the department ought to try to eliminate the problems confronting our Indian peoples, thereby doing away with the necessity for the department. I support that suggestion.
I have good friends in the department, and I learned something which those outside the department may not know but which is common knowledge within the department. It is epitomized in a reported conversation between two older members of the department. One said to the other, "Do you not find it strange that junior members of the department have not come forward with suggestions to alleviate some of the problems facing our Indians?" The reply was, "These juniors are acting as we acted 20 years ago when we were younger. They are afraid that if they bring forward too many suggestions and solve problems they may find themselves without jobs before retirement age." This story is not to be taken in a jocular manner because it exemplifies the feeling of some officials in the department. I do not criticize civil servants in general. In the Department of Indian Affairs we have some diligent, hard-working men, and excellent field men.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58 (11)-ALLEGED DENIAL OF FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS TO NATIVE INDIAN PEOPLE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58 (11)-ALLEGED DENIAL OF FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS TO NATIVE INDIAN PEOPLE
speechtext:
I could mention names but I will not. Yet it can be said, as the minister himself suggested, that many in the department adopt a paternalistic attitude to our Indian peoples. I think the hon. member for Skeena had all these matters in mind when he suggested that the minister ought to work toward abolishing his own ministry.
I was also pleased to hear the minister say that as a result of meetings he has attended
March 6. 1969	COMMONS
with Indian peoples he has concluded they are capable of speaking for themselves. That fact was proven conclusively during a meeting not long ago in Ottawa of the Indian Affairs Committee. It will be remembered that representatives of the Indian Brotherhood came to Ottawa for the sole purpose of forming a national Indian brotherhood, and they attended our committee meeting. I do not know whether the minister was there. The deputy minister, 1 believe, was there on that occasion, and with him were eight, nine or ten experts from the department. Those representatives questioned the deputy minister, and Members of Parliament on the committee directed questions at all the experts for about two hours.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Before the meeting concluded the chairman asked the representatives of the Indian Brotherhood if they would like to say a few words. I recall the words of Isaac Beaulieu who was representing the Manitoba Indian Brotherhood on that occasion. He stated he had heard a number of questions directed to the officials of the Indian Affairs Branch and heard a number of answers to the effect the department had been considering these problems but had been unable to arrive at an adequate solution.
Mr. Beaulieu was curious about the fact that the people in the Indian Affairs Branch had not been able to arrive at solutions and had not consulted with the officials of the Indian Brotherhood who represent the Indian people of Canada. Mr. Beaulieu's remarks were very timely and very much in line with what is taking place today. In many cases Indian problems are not being dealt with in the proper manner and not as quickly as they should be.
As the hon. member who initiated this debate rightfully said, we in the opposition parties have been asking the government for some time to set up the Indian Claims Commission. The minister is aware by this attendance at some of the consultation meetings in regard to changes in the Indian Act that the Indian people, including those representing Indian bands in Manitoba, have requested direct Indian representation on that claims commission. I do not know whether the minister has given the matter the consideration it deserves and has been able to convince his colleagues in the cabinet that Indian representation is desirable on the claims commission when it is set up.
DEBATES	6295
Alleged Denial of Rights of Native Indians
I want to go on record as saying that it is not only desirable but imperative that there be equal or majority representation of our native people on the Indian Claims Commission. The minister has stated today that the Indian people can speak for themselves. I assure the minister that we in the official opposition are not attacking the motives of the government, but we maintain that the government is not attacking the problems of the Indian people in a manner acceptable to the vast majority of Canadians or the Indian people concerned. I assume that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) and the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Andras) are sincere.
During the last election campaign I told the Indian people I would not criticize the previous government except for the course it took in relation to health services. I told them I would not criticize the sincerity of the government in regard to wanting to help the Indian people. As the minister mentioned, there is no doubt that those who speak today will give him some very frank ideas as to what should and can be done. We in the official opposition believe there is a genuine desire on the part of the government to improve the position of the Indian people of Canada, although I hasten to add that the government is not adopting the proper course. I accept that this is a most difficult problem. It is not our purpose to make it more difficult but to force the government to act as progressively as they have been talking. We expect the government to practise what they preach.
The minister stated that some delay has occurred in the continuation of the consultation meetings with respect to changes or amendments of the Indian Act and the setting up of the Indian Claims Commission. He stated that these delays were at the request of the Indian people. I accept that because I feel that the Indian people must be given an adequate length of time to digest thoroughly the plans of the government. In view of the fact the government and its predecessors for several years have said that an Indian Claims Commission would be set up, we feel this should be done as quickly as possible. The government is not being effective in Indian policy. There is disturbing evidence the government is not giving this matter priority. It should be near the top of the list of priorities. I will not get into a discussion at this time regarding the two constitutional conferences held during the last two years.
March 6. 1969

Alleged Denial of Rights of Native Indians

speechtext:
Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. I will attempt to be brief.
e (4:30 p.m.)
It is amazing to me that we can have discussions from one end of Canada to the other on subjects such as bilingualism and bicul-turalism, which I know are tremendously important, but how much importance has this house placed on the questions we have raised from time to time about the abrogation of Indian treaty rights? On occasion we have raised the abrogation of rights granted to our native Indian people by treaties entered into with them by the government of Canada. When we mention such matters we do not get much response from the government, and we do not get much attention from the news media. But just mention bilingualism or biculturalism and everyone plays it up. On the one hand, we are violating treaties; on the other hand, some people are trying to institute bilingualism across Canada. Without criticizing them I say we pay more attention to the desirability of bringing in something new than we do to the fact that the government has actually welshed on its agreements with the Indians. Let no one again use the phrase "just society" in Canada until the government gets around to correcting the situation that stems from the abrogation of Indian rights.
One of the principal examples is the abrogation of Indian hunting rights. The fact that certain conservationists feel that the Indian people should not have special privileges has nothing to do with the case. The Indians have treaty rights. Two Indians from my constituency had their cases taken right up to the Supreme Court of Canada, and on a five to four decision of the nine judges the Migratory Birds Convention Act was ruled to take precedence over Indian treaty rights. Regardless of which way the decision went, there were four judges who felt that the government was wrong in what it had done in relation to these treaty rights.

When the minister points out that the government is endeavouring to straighten out this very difficult problem I reply that these things can be straightened out provided he meets with the other authorities concerned. For the past four years I have been requesting that ministers sit down with their counterparts in the United States and renegotiate the Migratory Birds Convention so that Canada may be able to live up to its commitments to its Indian people. Many people will say that repeated mention of this problem takes up a lot of parliament's time, but I am sure Canada's reputation in the world at large would not be too good if we abrogated treaties with other countries. Let us show we have the desire to solve the problems of our native people by beginning immediately to solve this problem.
A little while ago the minister announced postponement of a major consultation conference scheduled for Ottawa, as was mentioned by the hon. member for Skeena. We hope it is a postponement and not a cancellation. The reason given for cancelling the meeting was that more time was needed to consider the material that had been presented. But many people believe this is not a valid reason. Some Indian people were highly critical of the representation they were granted at the conference, and indeed some spokesmen for the Indians of Alberta were so disturbed that they threatened to boycott the conference. Some meetings have already been held at various points across Canada, and we can only hope that after the final meeting the government will decide what changes it will propose in the Indian Act.
The Manitoba Indian Brotherhood has stated that one fact emerges most clearly from the meetings that have been held, namely, that the Indian people need and demand legislation that will change their present status from so-called protected wards of the government to equal citizenship with all other Canadians. Therefore they say that the Indian Act in its present form must be abolished because it is merely a catalogue of restrictions, and whatever the new legislation is called it must be more than a mere revision of the old act. The Indian people demand the destruction of all the old barriers and the provision of enlightened government action to provide opportunities whereby Indians, controlling their own destiny, can take their proper place in the Canadian mosaic. We in the official opposition will be anxiously awaiting an announcement from the minister that
March 6. 1969

the government is prepared to take the proper action.
I am sorry that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) is not able to be in the house at this time. I know he is busy having meetings with regard to a subject which I brought to his attention within the last few days.

I thank the minister. I am sure he realizes I was not criticizing the Minister of National Health and Welfare for not being here. e (4:40 p.m.)

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is about a year since we have had the opportunity to debate in the House of Commons the situation in respect of our native peoples. I believe it is only fair to say that the debate which has been going on so far today has been on the same non-partisan level which we have enjoyed in the past. I think we should also welcome the new minister to the list of ministers of this department. The Department of Indian Affairs has had more casualties than any other, I believe largely because of the inherent impossibility of the task the minister is given to perform.
March 6, 1969
6298	COMMONS
Alleged Denial of Rights of Native Indians
I should like to speak briefly about one area in which I believe the Department of Indian Affairs should be moving. I have some statistics concerning the progress made in the field of education in terms of the number of students now taking courses at the various educational levels. For example, in 1957-58 there were 124 post-secondary students. For 1967-68 that number has gone up to 225. The number of children in high schools in the same period has increased from 1,900 to 5,900. The number attending at the elementary school level is 48,000 now compared with 31,000 in 1957-58. I think this indicates a very laudable improvement.
There is, however, one aspect of the problem which bothers me considerably. Once the students leave school the Department of Indian Affairs seems to have very few support programs to assist them in taking their rightful place in society. Once an Indian has received an education he cannot go back to the sterile existence that he would have on the reserve. He must go into a world very different from that which he knew while at school or on the reserve. When he does, the Department of Indian Affairs has practically no program of assistance. The only program it has is a rather minor one involving Indian friendship centres.
In the whole of Canada there are only 21 of these centres, all of which are in provinces west of the Ontario-Quebec border. There are none in Quebec or the maritimes. The information I have from the Indian Affairs office indicates that in Ontario there are four which are located at London, Toronto, Parry Sound and Port Arthur. I know there is a friendship centre in Kenora, Ontario. Perhaps the statistics of the Department of Indian Affairs are not always up to date. The centre in Kenora has been unable to obtain any meaningful assistance. Their facilities are overcrowded and yet there is no program for a capital grant.
The type of program the federal government has to assist Indian friendship centres is ridiculous, to say the least. In the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta there are federal provincial agreements providing grants in amounts varying from $20,000 to $30,000 annually to each of these three provinces. In order to receive these grants the province must pay 50 per cent of the costs under a cost-sharing plan. These grants are designed to pay only the administration costs of the friendship centres. They do not cover


capital costs, hostel costs or even court worker costs.
In Ontario and British Columbia the friendship centres make their own approaches to the citizenship branch in Ottawa which makes matching grants equal to the provincial grants. However, the provincial and federal matching grants meet only two-thirds of the annual administrative costs. Therefore one-third of the annual administrative costs must be raised locally by each individual friendship centre. It seems to me this is a totally inadequate way to deal with a very serious problem. The bureaucratic system is probably the best way we have found to deal with problems through government action, but when we get into a situation where bureaucracy works against bureaucracy changes must be made quickly.
Indians who leave their reserves to seek work need help. Just as immigrants who have come to Canada have adopted the church hall type of program to assist them in becoming integrated into Canadian life, so too the Indian people need help. The Indian people are on a different basis from immigrants and it seems to me they need special help. When one is organizing Indian friendship centres it is difficult to get assistance at all from the federal government. There are individuals in the Indian Affairs and Citizenship Branches who do give some assistance but their efforts are often stopped by the department itself.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I want to give a specific example of the problem I am speaking about. In one town in my constituency, Red Lake, there is employment for Indians. Consequently Indians have come from all over North Western Ontario, from the northern areas of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and, I am told, even from Alberta, because there are jobs in the gold mines at Red Lake. There are not as many as before but there are some. A new iron mine in the area has made an effort to hire Indian labour.
The problem is that there is no housing and no organization to assist the Indians. There is nowhere they can go to receive help in integrating themselves into the new culture even though they are willing to do so. However, there is an organization there now called the Red Lake Indian Association which is trying to establish a friendship centre in the town of Red Lake where there is almost no serviced land. The township of Red Lake offered to provide serviced land to this organization at a cost of $1. A heating system has been offered
March G, 1969	COMMONS
by one of the local gold mines. Yet, there is no way in which either the federal government or the provincial government to this date can move and provide these people with the assistance they require.
In the new policy, which I hope the government will be announcing, I trust the tools that are required to enable the Indians to take their place in Canadian society will be provided. At the present time it seems to me that the educational program is adequate but the follow-up is simply lousy. A lot of work remains to be done and much imagination needs to be shown.
I should like to deal with some of the larger issues in what we term the Indian problem. My way of looking at it is to consider it not as an Indian problem but as a problem facing 230,000 people who have lived outside the mainstream of Canadian life and who are now trying to establish their place within the Canadian mainstream. It seems to me one of the primary things the federal government should do is to involve the provincial governments more deeply in Indian affairs. There are two reasons for this. First of all, there should be no distinction made between citizens of Canada. There should not be any necessity to provide separate services for Indians in, for example, the fields of education and medical services. However, the provinces will not be particularly willing to move into these areas, and one reason for this, I suggest, is the plight of the Metis.
If you begin to extend provincial services to the Metis it means that people, part Indian, part white, who for years have received no services from either the provincial government or the federal government, will receive provincial services. Therefore the cost to the provinces of these additional services for Indian people is not measured just by what the federal government pays in providing services to the Indian people, but also by the cost of extending such services to all these other people who have been ignored over a period of time. That, too, is part of the problem. It may well be that the federal government should look very carefully at this problem and integrate the Metis into programs that are designed for the Indian people. If the government does enter into negotiations with the provinces with a view to turning over these services and paying its share of the costs, it should also insist that the Metis be given their rightful share of fundamental rights that everybody in Canada enjoys and for which, incidentally, these people of Metis 29180-399

I also favour the decentralization of Indian affairs because I do not believe that the federal government is the source of wisdom in all things, particularly Indian affairs. I think there is much more conventional wisdom, if I may use that phrase, among the people living in communities which contain both whites and Indians. Often a far better relationship exists between them than exists between the Indians and the department.
When we talk about new policies for the Indian people I think we have to realize that much of what has been said in this house today does not apply to the Indian people who reside in the Northwest Territories, the Yukon, or in the constituency of Kenora-Rainy River. The people in my riding are not necessarily able to take advantage of all the programs available to them simply because they do not know how to cope with the white man's society. For example, it is only within the last ten years that roads have been built to some of the Indian communities that are close to white communities in my constituency. Only now are these people adjusting to the services that the Department of Indian Affairs and the provinces can now provide. Therefore it is absurd to assume that all Indian people are equally advanced and able to take advantage of all the opportunities we hope to provide to them. It seems to me that we require a far more flexible system that will offer a series of options and permit the Indians to opt in or opt out as they see fit. Perhaps it may be necessary for the government to set time limits, to establish quotas, to establish a timetable, so that when Indians at one level are prepared in order to move up to another level they can, but not to the disadvantage of others who many not be as advanced as they are.
Another aspect of the problem is that in my opinion there is a great deal of arrogance toward Indians in the House of Commons, and perhaps I am as guilty in this regard as anybody else. We seem to assume that we can formulate policies for our Indian people which they are going to follow. Although we pass the Indian Act it is the Indians themselves who should be deeply involved in the framing of its terms, even in its administration. It is the Indians who are affected by its provisions, not us. I detect a certain amount of arrogance in speeches that have been made on this subject that do not fit the facts, and I think we are all guilty of it.

I should like to give the house an illustration of the difficulties that we are going to have to face. In many areas there are going to be tremendous conflicts between the young people and the older generation. They will have to learn to govern themselves and resolve their own internal difficulties. The Indian Affairs Branch has been a very convenient scapegoat for many Indians. Because of the Indian Affairs Branch we have been unable to progress, say the Indians. Because of the Indian Affairs Branch, they say, we have not been able to govern ourselves.
If a new Indian Act is passed, as we hope it will be, this is going to mean that the Indians themselves will have to accept a great deal more responsibility for their own activities. Such a procedure will, I suggest, be difficult and slow. I do not think we can come up with any policy that is going to solve all the problems of the Indians in 100 years. I think that any government or legislative body that announces that it has a program to settle all Indian problems in 100 years flat is clearly not in touch with what is going on in the country and with what the Indian people are thinking. I sense this type of attitude among the members of the cabinet, though not so much on the part of the two ministers directly responsible. However, I get the feeling that the cabinet has decided that it is not going to do anything about solving the problems of the Indians until it is able to come up with a program that will solve the problems of the Indians in 100 years guaranteed. I think that is unrealistic.
I should like to see the Indian Act done away with because I believe it is an anachronism. Nevertheless, I understand that because of historic treaty rights and for other reasons we will have to have some form of Indian Act. We have to recognize that the original intention of the Indian Act was to provide protection for Indians. We have to continue to provide them with certain services. But the goal toward which we should work is that which the hon. member for Skeena suggested; the minister should work himself out of a job. But I think we have to face up to the realities of the situation.
I believe, that what the Department of Indian Affairs should be doing is helping the Indians to develop among themselves their own agencies that will work toward their own benefit. In the riding of Kenora-Rainy River there are a number of organizations, Indian corporations, that operate under an advisory body called the Amik Association. The Amik


Association has been receiving a grant of $15,000 from the provincial government, a sum shared jointly by the federal government. Because of the organization's success the grant has been upped to $24,000, again shared equally by the two governments.
The organization has prepared a very extensive and I think well thought-out brief for the Ford Foundation because it was not getting anywhere with the federal and provincial governments. It could get a little money to help meet administration costs but could not get the "seed" money it really required in order to go ahead with some of the projects it has in mind. So it submitted a brief to the Ford Foundation of America, which was accepted enthusiastically. The Ford Foundation wrote back and said: "We will put up $50,000 for a revolving loan fund for your area provided the federal and provincial governments will each put up $50,000." The money is to be used for "seed" projects.

It seems to me that here is an example of a great initiative by a group of local people, some white, some Indian, working sometimes in concert with and at other times in opposition to the Department of Indian Affairs and the other do-gooder organizations that involve themselves in Indian affairs. They came up with a proposal which they submitted to the federal and provincial governments. I think the two governments are on trial. I do not think they have any choice but to go ahead and provide the money to this organization which has proven itself to be effective. It is completely independently controlled; it is autonomous; it is on its own. I think the minister should look into this matter as soon as possible with a view to approving the program.
I would like to say a word or two about the consultative process. Quite frankly, I have not been happy with the way it has been carried out, particularly with the way it has affected the Indian people of my area. The concept of the consultation process has been that the Indian, like the white man, is used to the operations of the white man's institutions.

When I have consultations with the Indians, in the northern areas particularly, the chief will be telling me something and as he is speaking somebody, not a member of the band council necessarily, may interrupt him and make a correction or put

across another point of view. The chief will go back, reverse his stand, take that person's point of view into consideration, and go ahead. There is a sort of direct relationship here.
The consultation was imposed from the top down. The Indians were told to elect representatives and send them to the Lakehead or Toronto. They were taken out of their native areas and natural environment and put in a white man's situation. In this situation we expected them to provide us with proper information with regard to the Indians.
I admit that perhaps this is a little overdrawn, but I think the general idea is true. Far more work should have been carried out at the band level. There would have been far more understanding of the questions involved if this process had been carried out at the band level because the Indians would have known what matters were being raised. This is particularly true of Indians in rural and other areas where they are not in direct communication one with another. This was not done. To a large extent I think this was responsible for the first series of consultations not being as successful as we hoped they would be.
At this time I should single out the former minister of Indian Affairs, now the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Laing), for his initiative in setting up this program and for the work he did. If anybody could be said to be the father of consultations, it would be the present Minister of Public Works. Mind you, it was not a very pleasant form of consultation at times; sometimes it resembled a shouting match. Nevertheless, he believed in consultation and dialogue and went ahead and set it up.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I begin by saying that the minister had some good things to say today, especially when he announced that in future less paternalism would be displayed towards our Indian population since Indians are now able to speak for themselves. Frankly, some of us would take the minister's statements more seriously if we had not heard similar statements so often in the past. If my memory serves me correctly, the present minister is the fifth minister to hold the Indian Affairs portfolio since 1963. Former ministers were, I think, Mr. Favreau, Mr. Nicholson, the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Laing) and the minister responsible for regional development (Mr. Marchand). I may not be entirely accurate about the ministers who held the portfolio; yet, I think all this minister's predecessors made a speech almost exactly the same as the one he made today. The Indians of Canada will believe in the government's good intentions when they see actions taking the place of words.
I did not think I would ever agree with anything the premier of Saskatchewan said, but I must confess I agree with his assertion made in the provincial legislature in Regina yesterday that, with respect to our Indians, we are sitting on a time bomb. The St. Regis Indians have blockaded the bridge crossing their reservation. There is trouble at the Pas where the Indians have been picketing a health centre because they believe the person running it is displaying discriminatory attitudes. Then, we have the disgrace of Akaitcho Hall, Yellowknife, where the students are living under conditions that would not be tolerated by any other student group in this country. There, students 19, 20 and 21 years of age, are being treated as second class citizens. They are not allowed out in the evening without a written pass. They cannot go from the hospital to the gymnasium in the school

Alleged Denial of Rights of Native Indians without obtaining a written pass and giving it back to their superiors when they return. They cannot smoke or drink, even where the law permits them to do so. In addition, they need a special permit to visit the old part of Yellowknife. Why is that, Mr. Speaker? Other Indians live in the old part of town, and the students need special permission before going there. The minister has had sufficient time to investigate what is going on in Akaitcho Hall. The difficulties there continue because many in this country believe that Indians are not as good as the rest of us. When the minister allows the current situation there to continue, he helps to foster the kind of thinking prevalent among some sections of our community. No wonder our Indians are concerned about what is happening.
I am ashamed that a magistrate of my city who sees Indians in court every day, and deals with their alleged infractions of the law, saw fit to appear on the national television program the "Public Eye" and make the statement reported in a letter that Chief Courchene sent. According to the letter, Magistrate Rice said;
I have never come across a married Indian Couple... There is something in their blood, I don't know what it is but an Indian and alcohol just don't mix ... An Indian woman told me-I guess she was an Indian, I can't tell the difference between an Indian and a Metis-if abortions were allowed she would have to have an abortion every morning.
In view of statements like these, is it any wonder our Indians are becoming restless, that they are beginning to demonstrate and that we face the possibility of violence? I suggest that the time for talk is over and the time for action has arrived.
The fifth annual review of the Economic Council shows that the life expectancy of the average Indian woman in Canada is 25 years, compared with 64 years for the rest of our population. Most Indians in Canada enjoy incomes of less than $3,000 a year and half our Indians enjoy incomes below $2,000 a year. Many Indians in this country live in poverty, and not much help is being extended to them. All these facts are well known.
Although it is important for us to know of the activities of the Indian Claims Commission, it is more important for us to know whether the government will act to help our Indians. Will it eliminate or reduce the bureaucracy which has directed every facet of Indian life here for more than 100 years? Will it allow Indians to decide what is good

I have travelled extensively in this country and am aware of many Indian problems. I know Indian leaders in Manitoba, Alberta and in northwestern Ontario. The house resumed consideration of the motion (Mr. Howard):
That in the opinion of this House the government, in spite of successive admissions of its failure to deal adequately with the various social and economic problems confronting our native Indian people, is following a course which threatens to perpetuate the denial of fundamental human rights and freedoms, to continue the destructive effects of paternalism, and to maintain discrimination based upon a cultural inheritance together with a general negation of human dignity and respect for our native people.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to make a few remarks in this debate about the native peoples. I should also like to commend the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) for introducing this motion. It is a good indication of the concern that all members of parliament have about the plight of the Indian peoples. I should say too that Canadians in all walks of life have never been more concerned about them. This is a good thing because, as has been generally known, the native peoples face some very great difficulties. The standard of living of too many of the Indian people in respect of income, health, housing, and other factors is much lower than is acceptable to the Canadian people. It would be useless, however, to dwell at
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Bechard),]
great length on all things that are wrong. I think many of the wrongs have been pointed out pretty adequately today by hon. members on both sides of the house.
The Minister of Indian Affairs, and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) gave an excellent address today. I think he presented a balanced picture of what the situation is today and what the government is trying to do to alleviate the conditions under which many of the Indian people are living. There are many, many good things the Indians are doing in addition to the many things that are wrong. I think the minister pointed this out as well in his remarks.
I should like to deal with a few of the remarks that were made today by some hon. members. The hon. member for Skeena referred to the problem as a fungus growth that is still growing and getting worse all the time, indicating that no progress has been made. I reject his suggestion that the Indian people are a fungus growth.

Then, why did you
not listen to what I said?
I did. I know the hon. member did not mean that some of us are fungi, but nevertheless the inference is there.
That is not true.

It is a
ridiculous statement and I reject it. The department is dealing with Indians. I think the hon. member should perhaps consider his choice of words. Under any circumstances, I reject the statement.

I rise on a matter of order, Mr. Speaker. I know the hon. gentleman wants to be truthful and correct. He is not being so in this instance. I do not want to become involved in a dialogue with him about it. What I said was that when, in 1867, the Fathers of Confederation decided that Indians on the land reserved for Indians should be under the exclusive jurisdiction of the federal parliament they started a program of paternalism. It is that paternalism that is the fungus growth which is still growing. I reject any implication on the part of the hon. member that I said otherwise.

I also reject the suggestion that we are not making any progress. Indians today are on the move as they have never been before. They are participating more and more in Canadian life
March 6, 1969

than they have ever done before. This is a good thing. We must participate as people in all aspects of Canadian life, economic, social and political. I should like to point out some examples of the progress the Indian people are making. These are not propaganda items from the Department of Indian affairs, as has been suggested by some hon. members. These are things the Indians are doing themselves. I have a clipping from the Financial Post dated August 10, 1968. The headline reads "Squamish Indians' enterprise transforms wasteland into profitable trailer park". The article goes on to say:
While some Indians across Canada are campaigning without much success for aboriginal land rights or seeking special concessions and compensation, Dan Baker, member of the council of the Squamish Indian tribe, has found that self-help and free enterprise can be far more satisfying-and profitable.
Dan, whose brother Simon is chief of the tribe, was inspired two years ago with what seemed at the time to be an almost impossible idea. The Squamish band for many years has held a strip of waterfront land facing Burrard Inlet, opposite Vancouver, some of which is now under lease to the municipalities of West Vancouver and North Vancouver.
At a point where the Capilano River, which rises in the North Shore mountains, meets tidewater near the Lions Gate bridge, there was a strip of timbered flat land undeveloped and apparently unwanted.
To Dan Baker the situation spelled opportunity. Wouldn't this be a wonderful location for a trailer park? The more he thought about it, the more he was impressed with the possibilities.
The land lies just across the Capilano River from the prestigious Park Royal area with its complex of high-rise apartments, shopping centres, specialty shops, theatres.
When Baker, with some encouragement from the federal Indian Affairs Department, made a modest start in clearing a part of the land for his trailer park, discriminating residents of West Vancouver, including members of the municipal council, were slightly aghast.
All that was several months ago. Today, it is obvious that Dan Baker's Capilano Mobile Park is an asset instead of any eyesore. Baker himself, his fellow tribe members and North Shore municipal officials are happy.
Because of the exacting standards set for intending residents-individual trailers cost from $8,000 to more than $20,000-the community has appealed only to people of means, many of them retired or semi-retired, who like the idea of living beside the river, in a dwelling free from the discomforts of apartment life and the inconvenience and high cost of maintaining conventional homes.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
The land is leased by Baker and his partner, Roger Battryn, from the Capilano band on a three-year renewable permit, and the band receives 10 per cent of the gross revenue from the project, which represents a total investment of about $100,000.

In so far as education is concerned, more Indians are being educated than ever before, and more and more of them want to be educated. They want to be educated along with other Canadians, and this is being done.
I remember that when I went to university there were only three or four of us attending the University of British Columbia. That was in 1955. Today, Mr. Speaker, there are some sixty members of various Indian bands in British Columbia attending the University of British Columbia. I think this is progress. The hon. member for Skeena says that nothing is being done, that no progress is being made. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, the Indian people are on the move today as they have never been before.
I am not going to sing the praises of the government for its treatment of the Indian peoples. Successive governments have failed to do the job that was required of them. But I do not want always to dwell on the things that have been wrong in the past. We must address ourselves resolutely to the future.
I paid tribute in my maiden speech, Mr. Speaker, to the right hon. gentleman for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) for giving the Indians the vote. This was one of the great decisions that the right hon. gentleman made during his time as Prime Minister. I also said, Mr. Speaker, and I would like to repeat, that more was done for the Indian people by the government of the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson than was done at any other time in our history. I would like to just list a few of those things to refresh the memories of hon. members on the other side.
Mr. Pearson's government announced a $112 million housing program. Loans from C.M.H.C. were made available for Indians to build houses on the reserves. An off-reserve housing program was introduced. I spoke to many, many Indians about this in various parts of the country, especially in British Columbia where this program was welcomed and has helped them a great deal to find a new life in the cities where other Canadians are living.
Federal spending in the years 1962-63 on Indian affairs was about $51 million. Federal spending in the years 1968-69 is almost $140 million. I think this is progress. I think it indicates the government's concern about the

I agree with many hon. members who have said that the objective of all members must be to work for the minister of Indian affairs in order to see that he works himself out of a job. It is basically wrong that there should be a department of government devoted to a particular race of people.
I would welcome the abolition of the department of Indian affairs and the Indian Act. There should not be special status in Canada for any group of people. There should not have to be special laws saying that I am an Indian. We are all Canadians.
But, Mr. Speaker, I think it is unrealistic that we should expect the Indian Act to be abolished right now. This is not the wish of the Indian people. The impression that I get from them is that they would like to see progressive options made available in the Indian Act until they can get on their feet, do many things for themselves and function as communities on the same basis as many other communities.
The hon. member for Skeena talked about consultations and meeting the wishes of the Indian people. At another point he said that the government should abolish the department of Indian affairs. I am not sure what he means, Mr. Speaker, I do not understand this type of language. The minister of Indian Affairs made it pretty clear that we are consulting the Indian people as widely as possible on the changes that they want in the Indian Act. This is a good thing and I welcome it. Never before in history have such wide consultations been held to amend a portion of the Indian Act or the Indian Act in total. The Indian people have been very concerned that everything was coming from the top, being fed down to them and handed to them as a fait accompli. I am glad to say that this is no longer the case. I am confident that when the new policy on Indian Affairs is announced, the new act is introduced and the claims bill is introduced, the wishes of the Indian people will be reflected therein.
The hon. member for Skeena also quoted several figures in regard to average age at death, and in the same breath was talking about life expectancy. If the figures that the hon. member was using are true, I should be almost dead. I want to assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I think I still have a few years left.

speechtext: If not, the average would be still lower.

To
clarify the record, average age at death reflects the age at which a certain number of persons die. Life expectancy reflects the average number of years of life for those who are still living. For example, if one person of 80 and a one year old baby die, the average age at death is about 40. If an 80 year old person and two one year old twins die, the average age at death is roughly 27. To clarify the record further, Mr. Speaker, the life expectancy of Indian men is 59.61 years at birth; life expectancy of non-Indian men at birth is 63.35 years. Life expectancy of Indian women at birth is 63.23 years; life expectancy of nonIndian women at birth is 74.17.

When I am finished. Statistics can often be misleading, and I am sorry to say that misleading statistics have often been used against the department of Indian affairs when it has been convenient for hon. members to suggest how bad things are. When the report on Indians and the law came out there was a story in one newspaper to the effect that 100 per cent of the women in the Kamloops jail were Indians. I was very alarmed at this statistic and I phoned Mr. Gus Godfriedson, an old friend in Kamloops, to ask what was going on and whether this was a true figure. He said, "Not that I am aware of. I know of one woman who has been in jail in Kamloops from time to time. If you call that 100 per cent, I guess the figure is correct."
With the best intentions in the world, members wound the Indian people when they use such figures. We are a proud people and there are many things that work against us. But most of them are not intentional, and we would hate to feel that they are.
As I have said before, the Indians have many accomplishments of which they can justly be proud. Most of us know that from time to time the department is a help. On the other hand, from time to time the department is not as helpful as we would like it to be. In our emotional moments many of us may blame the department for many things. But if we are to debate the future of the Indian people on an adequate basis, we will have to recognize that many things are being done by the Indian people. Many things are being done by various agencies of government, including the Indian Affairs branch. Still more things

remain to be done. But most Indian people today know that things are very different from what they were. Those who read the record of this debate will surely feel that members on all sides of the house want to do a better job for them.

Mr. Speaker,
I appreciate very much the statement of the hon. member who spoke before me, but nevertheless we much understand that within his party the hon. member may feel a little too bound to defend party policy. Certainly he is right to rejoice over the fact that we now appear willing to give a final solution to the Indian problem.
But if we consider the present situation that was permitted to develop for many years, not to say centuries, we should wonder what will be the results of the new government policy. Why? Because the situation has become so serious that one wonders if it might not be too late for a solution.
I would now like to make a comparison between the fate of as important a minority as the French Canadians and that of the Canadian Indians. We French Canadians have been fighting since 1760 against complete assimilation, against the loss of our rights and prerogatives. We are in a position to understand the problems of a race doomed to extinction, judging by the views which have been prevailing for a long time in this government.
So I can well understand the Indian problem. The principle according to which everyone should be allowed to remain himself is so true and enriching in a country like Canada that every effort should have been made in the past to make sure that the Indians, the first and most important inhabitants of our country, remain themselves.
The government is now trying to correct the situation and if the Indians themselves believe that this will be successful, I am the first to be delighted about it.
I doubt it, but this day may have helped in finding a real and definite solution to the problem.
I would also like to speak about the problems of the Eskimos, especially those living in northern Quebec. Even if it is now possible to give them the means to be independent, we should not prevent them from leading a fuller

So, if the Eskimos are ready to look after their own affairs, to invest their profits to their advantage in their own region, that could be a partial solution to the problem.
Consequently, foreign companies, and more particularly American companies, should not be allowed to take over the implementation of those contracts, to make profits and invest them in the States or in a country other than Canada, above all when Eskimos can run their business by themselves to their own profit. Apart from being an incentive for employment in those areas, the implementation of those contracts would enable the Eskimos to make money, as the Americans have always done. That would make them more independent, freer, for they would no longer have to make do with the welfare allowances that they get at the present time.
All those problems should therefore be considered in a very open way and we should not give with one hand what we take with the other. If we really want the Indians or the Eskimos to enrich our national heritage, we should let them have their own way and facilitate their self-determination, by all possible means.

The hon. gentleman is from a riding neighbouring mine. I know that his interest in the Indian people is genuine, deep, and of every long standing. Listening to him tonight, I did not find that his language matched the slightly intemperate tone of the motion itself. I found him generally non-partisan, very fair for the
