He is one of the people in this house who took an interest in what has come to be called the Indian problem while numerous other Canadians, who at times now take a somewhat noisy interest in the matter, were quite silent and indifferent. If I start on a slightly critical note in reviewing what the hon. member for Skeena said, it is because I am leading up to a point. I should like to refer to one section of his remarks in which he was criticizing the booklet "Choosing a Path" which was distributed to the consultative groups as they met across Canada. The hon. member referred to the section which asked the Indians what they thought of the Indian liquor legislation. He went on to ask: Isn't this ridiculous? How many times have they been asked this question? Could they be blamed if they looked upon it as an insult to their intelligence?
Can we really say this, Mr. Speaker? It is true that they have been asked this question many times. It is true also that they have given many different answers. This does not apply only to Indians. The white people of Canada have, for many generations, asked this question about liquor control. They have given many different answers. They are continuing to give different answers.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
In my own province of British Columbia, the provincial government has recently set up another royal commission to investigate the problem of drinking in the province. So, I do not really think that it is an insult to the intelligence of Indians to ask them the question once again, or if it is, it is at least no more insulting than referring the question to yet another royal commission on behalf of the white community. I am not bringing this up to niggle on a small point but to lead to a point which I think is important, and it is this: There is disagreement among the white community in this nation on many issues, and there is disagreement among the Indian community on many issues. It is a good thing that there is. Occasionally, during the course of this debate I have heard mention of this figure called "the Indian" as though every Indian in Canada were somehow merged into a single recognizable entity. This mythical figure we call "the Indian" expresses the unanimous collective thoughts of all the Indians in Canada. This is a false premise and as

DEBATES	March 6, 1969
long as we persist in it in our handling of the important matters of Indian administration, administration by Indians themselves or by the Indian department, we cannot be right. There is no such man as "the Indian" in Canada. Indians are people of immense variety, and there is no reason why they should not disagree. It is true that, for instance, in most of the provinces of Canada there is a single Indian organization. Speaking in terms of fairly large organizations, there are at least four different Indian organizations in British Columbia which have slightly different views on what the course of their people should be. Occasionally these organizations are viewed somewhat critically by the white community. They say: "Why don't you people combine? Why can't you speak for British Columbian Indians with a single voice?"
Some of the people who ask this question sit in this house where there happen to be four political parties, not one of which is in total agreement with any other party. If it is right for us, then it is also right for the Indian, and this leads us a little further. It leads to the question of consultation with the Indians. Let us, and let the minister, recognize the fact that we cannot consult with the Indians of Canada and get one, single, cohesive answer as to what they want. In fact, it is almost an insult to suggest that we can go to the Indians from one side of this nation to the other asking: "Tell us what you want" and assuming that they are all going to tell us the same thing, therefore, it is merely a matter of meeting their requests in greater or lesser degree. This is not to happen. There are great variations even within a single area in my own riding of Coast-Chilcotin. I made a rough calculation a short time ago and I found that there were over 30 reserves in my riding. Many of the people cannot converse with one another except through the medium of the English language because their own languages are of such a vastly different nature.
In the course of the consultation meetings, how many points of view have been put forward on how the Indians feel as to their role as citizens of Canada, citizens of the province, citizens of North America and citizens of what might be called a pan-Indian society? In each case there are at least four distinct views held by the Indians. I should like to quote one from a publication called the "Indian Magazine" which I am sure many hon. members who are interested in this subject
March 6, 1969	COMMONS
receive. Let us see what Chief Max Gros-Louis of Huron Village near Quebec city had to say:
X can't see the Indians belonging to the provinces, because there's going to be another separation among Indians. We are already separated by the United States. Now if we start separating by provinces, that's going to be the end of the Indian.
That is one man's view. The consultative group has heard from Indians who positively want to be citizens of the province in which they reside. They feel that this is of prime importance to them. They feel that in many provinces of Canada they are being deprived, in greater or lesser degree, of basic rights as provincial citizens. There is a third view among Indians which is that the international border is an artificial line; that it is one which should not apply to them and that the Indian society is not of the nation of Canada nor of the nation of the United States but is a loosely connected society of a single group based on a single culture whose home is North America. There is yet a fourth view held that within Canada the Indian people are not Canadians but are allies of the British Crown; that they are a nation separate within Canada and that their true connection is to the Royal House of Britain.
I am not going to suggest which of these views predominates amongst Indians. I have some ideas, but I do not know whether it is up to me to suggest them at this time. However, I would point out that every one of these views has some legitimacy and every one of them has some followers in Canada. Therefore, whenever I hear that any man, particularly a white man but also an Indian, claims that he knows what all the Indian people of Canada really want, my faith in his knowledge and judgment is diminished. I bring this point forward in connection with the delays in bringing forth the new Indian act and the legislation for an Indian claims commission.
There is one difference between the present administration of the Indian department and those which preceded it. I think it is that we are attempting consultation with the Indian. As the hon. member for Skeena said, we have always claimed we were consulting them, but did we really do it? I can quote a good friend of mine in this regard, Chief Dan George of the Burrard No. 3 reserve. I recall him saying once: "Oh yes, the white man is always coming around and he says to us 'what do you want' but he never waits for us to answer".

Those replies are going to come slowly but surely if we are committed to asking questions and waiting for answers. Then, we cannot arbitrarily say: "Sorry, you are too long in giving your answer. I would not pretend to criticize the record of Canadian white governments in their handling of Indian affairs but at the same time, though speaking from less experience because the period of my close association as a member of parliament has been briefer, I would not attempt to defend all the actions of the present Indian Affairs branch. Like the hon. member for Skeena I have the feeling that it is shot through with a very strong degree of paternalism, and this cannot be good; it must go. I certainly agree that the earlier the Indian Affairs branch can bring about conditions in which it is no longer required, the better it will be for the Indians. There is, however, a point on which I am not clear, though I listened carefully to the hon. member for Skeena in this respect. He was speaking of the Indian Act and it was not clear to me whether or not he was recommending that the Act be abolished. I would be delighted if he would interrupt me and tell me whether or not he advocates the abolition of the Indian Act.
Yes.

I wish I could understand his position; I am sure he will answer me on some occasion. I cannot understand it, now. I, too, would like to see the Indian Act abolished but we must realize that we have certain obligations to the Indians of this country by treaty. Some of these treaties we have bent, and others we have broken. Then, as hon. members are aware, there are Indians in British Columbia with whom we have never signed treaties of any kind. Nevertheless, since we have signed treaties and assumed responsibilities to these people, how are these

I think the Indian people must themselves surrender these special rights voluntarily. We have no right unilaterally to push aside these agreements and wipe this legislation off the books. It seems to me that whether we call it an Indian Act or something else, we must keep legislation respecting the special rights of the Indian people on the law books of this country until and unless they themselves choose to ask that it be removed.
Right again. Yes.
Am I to understand that the hon. member would be satisfied with a change in the name of the act?
I would say, "no" to that one.

There is one other point I should like to raise, and I feel it involves a moral responsibility on the part of the white majority in this country. There are many Indians who wish to leave the reserves, move into white society and integrate completely, losing their Indian identity. This should be their right. Since in most cases they are disadvantaged people, I believe we have a duty to give them special help in this regard. But what of the Indians who wish to remain Indians, who wish to live on their reserves and lead the traditional lives of their people? Is this not also their right? Do they not have the right, if they choose, to continue to exist as a separate, non-integrated group in Canadian society? It seems to me that both by treaty and in terms of ordinary justice the Indians who choose to remain Indians have the right to do so. Does this necessarily place them in the position of being second class citizens? I believe that throughout most of our history this has been the effect. By choosing to live on the reserves, by choosing to retain the old ways, they have tended to become second class citizens. Surely, the Canadian nation can find some way of guaranteeing that these people can live different lives without obliging them to be poor for the most part, as they are, or poorly educated, or discriminated against in any real way because they are Indians.
Surely, out of our present examination of the Indian Act the most important thing we can bring forward is a recognition on the part of the government, on the part of civil servants and on the part of the ordinary people

of Canada that when we meet an Indian we are meeting a person, one individual. And there is every bit as much variety among people of Indian ancestry as there is among people of any other race.
Before I close, I should like to comment on one point made by the hon. member for Skeena. I should like to give my fullest support to his plea for the early setting up of an Indian claims commission. Let us not fool ourselves. The government of this country has neglected to sign treaties such as the Jay Treaty and Treaties 8 and 11 in the north. We have made treaties and broken them. We have failed to make treaties in British Columbia west of the rockies, and in other parts of the north with the Eskimos. This record of doubtful faith, and in some cases of bad and broken faith, is a festering sore in this country. Let us not delay any longer than is necessary before forming an Indian claims commission to review these old disagreements, to patch up old difference and to start us in the 1970s with some of the old hatred and bitterness wiped away. I thank the house for its attention.
Hear, hear.

In the past several years, Mr. Speaker, certain changes have taken place in the attitude of Canadians toward the Indian population of this country. Public opinion has been aroused. It has been noticed, perhaps as a result of some publicity, that the Indian people are living in conditions which are not comparable with those experienced by non-Indian Canadians. There is an obvious disparity in their means of living in all aspects-a disparity in housing, in economic status, in opportunities for education, and in opportunities to seek the better things which this country has to offer.
As a result of this change in public opinion under the pressure which has been building during the past couple of years, the Indian affairs branch has decided to take a closer look at the Indian Act in its various aspects and to establish whether some of the difficulties which the Indian people experience today may not be correlated with certain aspects of this legislation. I think it is fair to say that public opinion has become aroused because our Indian population in general is becoming more educated. The more educated Indians have become outspoken and have brought their problems to the attention of the Canadian public.

It should not be surprising that they are as diverse in their capacities, their orientations and their objectives as any other similar sized sampling of people.

It seems to me that in this approach to Indians as a unit, the fallacy in our entire policy of the past lies. The fatal flaw of our Indian legislation since its inception has been this idea of considering Indians as a unit, rather than people the same as the rest of us. We are fundamentally wrong when we try, in a particular piece of legislation, to deal with all Indians as though they were a homogenous group, because we attempt to identify an average Indian to whom we can relate the legislation when there is really no such thing.
Having done that, we compound the felony, motivated I am sure, by compassion rather than colonialism, by reducing that average Indian to some sort of lowest common denominator to be sure that we do not treat any unjustly in a material sense, and in the process we treat almost all Indians unjustly in the spiritual sense.
The philosophical dilemma is far from new. I will refer here to the House of Commons debates in 1880, volume 2 at page 1990 and 1991. On the one side of the debate Mr. White of East Hastings said in part:
We are making them believe that the country will support them, and putting them in a position in which they have no credit or standing in the community. We should no longer treat the Indians as children. Something should be done to put them in a position to make them know and feel that they were responsible to themselves and to the country.
On the other side of the debate, Sir John A. Macdonald said:
You cannot make an agriculturalist of the Indian. All we can hope for is to wean them, by slow degrees, from their nomadic habits, which have almost become an instinct, and by slow degrees absorb them or settle them on the land. Meantime they must be fairly protected.
That was in 1880. Today, almost 90 years later, the same points of view exist.
The fact remains that Indians are now what is fashionably called, "a visible minority". Policies carried on by governments since the first Indian Act was enacted by the United Provinces of Canada in 1865 have made them basically welfare cases. Because they are a visible minority they are visible welfare cases. There is a stigma to that status, and whether or not we are or should still be obsessed by the guilt that was expressed in the debates of 1880, it seems we must now redirect the legislation and the policy behind it. We must abandon paternalism no matter how

Above all, we must orient our policy and the administration of it to individuals, to people, not to norms or averages, because when you deal with human beings there are really no norms or averages. The typical or average Indian is a fiction, a creation of administrative convenience. Continuation of the concept will invalidate any policy, however well conceived in its other dimensions.
I am heartened that even with the handicaps of the existing legislation the present minister and his department appear to have taken a human and a personal view towards the Indians, towards their responsibility. I have every confidence that in the new legislation coming before us as a result of the consultations that are going on today our policy for the Indians will be based on compassion and not paternalism, consultation not direction, and participation not dictation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I start by apologizing to any members on the other side whom I may have displaced in rising. May I also join many previous speakers in expressing appreciation at the high tone of the debate that has taken place today. This has been one of the more constructive debates it has been my pleasure to hear in this house. There have been 12 or 13 speakers in the debate this afternoon and this evening, every one of whom I believe has added something constructive to the review and to the considerations we must give in formulating a new policy. I do not think I can cover all of the highlights of the speech of each hon. member, but I will attempt to reply in general and to answer quickly one or two questions.
The immediately preceding speaker, known as "Weasel Horse", the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Gundlock), expressed concern at the delay in the national consultation meeting. In the interests of saving time, may I simply refer him to the remarks of my colleague the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) earlier today, and also assure the hon. member that we are giving consideration to the question of the number of representatives from Alberta. Some difficult problems are posed but we are going to be very open minded and do all we can to satisfy all concerned. I am sure that, with good will on all sides, a reasonable solution will be found.
The hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Mahoney), pointed out one rather agonizing section of the Indian Act which by itself, if for no other reason, indicates the great need for change. The hon. member referred to the Indian child who misses school occasionally
March 6. 198S
6320	COMMONS DEBATES
Alleged Denial of Rights of Native Indians and is automatically labelled a juvenile delinquent without due process of law.
The hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yew-chuk) had some worthwhile comments to make, though too many for me to refer to them all. He referred to the need for family planning. I was impressed by the way he put it, that we should ask the Indian people what they wanted, rather than in any sense imposing something upon them. He also referred to flying doctors. I think it is fairly well known that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) has been negotiating with the Canadian Medical Association and with regional and provincial medical associations to see whether a voluntary roster system could be instituted that would bring better service to Indian communities in more remote areas.
The hon. member for Coast Chilcotin (Mr. St. Pierre) made reference to the various differences of opinion existing among Indian people from coast to coast. I hope to refer to his rather interesting comments later.
The hon. member for Kamloops-Cariboo (Mr. Marchand) made a very pertinent observation when he talked of the need for all of us to recognize the great progress that is being made by many Indian people. So often in watching television I am concerned that, while undeniably poverty among the Indian people is shown, and while unfortunately there is a high rate of alcoholism and a rising rate of crime among the Indian people, a balanced picture is not presented. The other side of the coin, is not shown indicating the great progress that has been made by more and more of our Indian people. I think it is important that we give a balanced picture, and certainly that was one of the many contributions the hon. member made in his remarks.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) made several constructive suggestions with which I cannot deal in detail. One of them was the thought-a thought that we are considering-that there should be established Indian development corporations; that there is a general need for decentralization and for economic development as a whole. I also join with the hon. member in expressing my distaste of what I saw on the television program "The Public Eye" to which he referred, when a rather prominent citizen made such a bigoted comment about Indians, their blood content, and their difficulties with alcohol. I think this program made all of us

who are at all sensitive to the situation cringe.
The hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Simpson) and others referred to the need for a higher priority to be given by the government in meeting the problems of our native Indian people.
Hon. members will probably be surprised to hear me say that the motion that began this debate is a good one. I think the wording is appropriate and set the tone of the debate, which has stayed on a fairly high plane.
The corollary to this motion is for the government, I hope helped by the opposition, to not pursue a course, whether innocently, mistakenly or deliberately, that will meet the objectives and cause the results that are inherent in the words contained in the motion. We must, of course, remove and eliminate the destructive effects of paternalism by removing paternalism. We must eliminate discrimination, and discrimination there is in this country. In our course of action, we must restore human dignity, respect, pride and self-confidence to a group of people who have been alienated by many factors, not the least of which have been the policies of the past.
In his elaboration the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) went back-and this is what has impressed me most of all in this debate-to examine the basic assumptions upon which our policy should be founded. He questioned those basic assumptions in the comments or partial solutions that he offered.
Specifically the criticism that is inherent in the motion before us today is contained in an expression of cynicism as to whether the government is going to take action. All I would say about that is that personally I am absolutely convinced that it will not be very long before action is taken and that there will be a constructive change in policy. I appreciate the fact-and many people have made this point today-that it is no longer a time for sweet words and speeches; it is a time for action.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
The other inherent criticism in the motion, referred to by the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Simpson) and others, was the delay in announcing policy. I, and I know my colleague the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and other colleagues in the cabinet, are also impatient to take the necessary action and to move on this whole situation. When my colleague the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
March 6, 1969	COMMONS
and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) discussed with me the assignment to work with them in identifying the problems and to recommend to them and the cabinet possible avenues for change, I felt it was necessary to charge out because, in the first place, one of the more specific matters to accomplish was the immediate revision of the Indian Act.
The first meeting which I attended, in Yellowknife last July, taught me very quickly that perhaps speed was required but haste was not a good idea. There were many aspects of this whole situation that had to be examined in depth after consultation with and listening to the views of Indian people. I think the real point is that we must move on a timetable that is acceptable to the Indian people. We must not try to meet some artificial deadline that might be suggested, and in the process fail to apply the wisdom that the situation needs after 300 years of neglect and incorrect policies.
I think it would be presumptuous of us as a government if, after seven months of consultation with Indian people across this country and an exchange of views such as we had in the consultations ending only four or five weeks ago, we had presented immediately to this house, the Indian people and the nation a package policy. If we had done that, I think it would have indicated to all concerned that we had made up our minds long ahead of time and were not really listening to the recommendations and points of view expressed during the 17 consultation meetings just ended. We had to have time and we must continue to take the time, to digest all the views and opinions expressed in the last eight months. I cannot see the wisdom or value to anybody in proceeding with a new policy without the input that is necessary from all these consultation meetings.
There has been criticism of the consultation meetings. I think the degree of criticism is in many ways far from justified. These meetings were far from perfect, but we should not go to the other side of the spectrum and say they were hopeless, useless or, as some have said, a facade. They were open meetings. It may have been specifically said that the purpose of the consultation meetings was simply to examine the proposed revisions of the Indian Act. But from the very first meeting, and in every subsequent meeting, there was no attempt on anybody's part, whether he was a minister or not, to suppress any point of view expressed about any matter bothering the Indian delegates who attended.
DEBATES	6321
Alleged Denial of Rights of Native Indians
These meetings covered the whole range of local problems, regional problems, national problems, the Indian's suspicion of government, their cynicism, treaty rights' and aboriginal rights; in fact, the whole gamut and range of frustrations and grievances that has built up over the centuries in respect of the non-Indian, Indian relationship. So, there was no suppression. Although these meetings may not have reached all the objectives we might have had in mind, I think it was a very valuable exercise and within a short time there will be in the policies that will be announced some indication of the value that came from those meetings.
As most hon. members know, there were 17 meetings. I believe all but one of them was attended by a minister, either my colleague the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development or myself. Of the 17 meetings I know my colleague was at eight, and I was at ten. There was only one, in Prince George, which we regret we did not attend. This was due to circumstances which arose very suddenly and could not be avoided.
There are in this country 558 Indian bands, and in those 17 consultation meetings 530 were represented. I think that is a pretty good representation. This brings to mind one of the problems we face and with which we must deal. We must have understanding in this respect, and perhaps some adjustment from the Indian people themselves. The hon. member for Kcnora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid) referred to the fact that Indian people do not view representation, the delegation of authority and the appointment of spokesmen, in the same manner as non-Indians. I have learned during the last few months that there is a tendency in the Indian community to seek consensus and unanimity. Often no one person is designated as the spokesman for a group of people. Often at these consultation meetings an Indian delegate would rise right at the beginning, to make it clear, and say: I speak for myself. In their gentle, effusive and humble way they would indicate that they were not taking unto themselves the authority to speak on behalf of other people.
There were many things wrong with the consultation meetings. There was insufficient opportunity for the Indians to consult amongst themselves beforehand, I think we have learned a great deal from that. At the same time, I think it was an exercise in consultation the like of which has never before been conducted by any government with any group of people in this country.
March 6, 1969
6322	COMMONS
Alleged Denial of Rights of Native Indians
We are embarking upon new policies. New policies will succeed, obviously, only if we insist in seeking the right answers with clarity and consistency in both the definition of the objectives we are seeking and the selection of the means of realizing them. In this process we must all ask ourselves certain basic, fundamental questions. Then, we have to try and answer those questions. Hopefully, from the questions and the answers will come enlightened policy. Some of these questions are: In what way are Indians excluded from our society? In what ways have they been disadvantaged? How did they come to be that way? What obstacles stand in the way of their achieving equal citizenship and full participation? Then the obvious question is: What actions and measures can be expected to overcome these obstacles?
I think in answering these questions it is important to examine the jurisdictional, legal, administrative, social and economic factors which shape the present status of Indian people and native peoples in our society. We must look at the special legal status of these people. We must recognize and consider the poverty aspects involved, their alienation, cynicism, mistrust of government and obvious isolation from the larger society.
The hon. member for Skeena referred this afternoon to the supposed basis for federal government acceptance of responsibility in this field. He referred to section 91, paragraph 24, of the British North America Act, which assigns the making of laws, of legislation respecting "Indians and lands reserved for the Indians" to the jurisdiction of the federal government. I do not know that this, to the exclusion of change, means that it has to be totally, utterly and exclusively the responsibility of the federal government and under its jurisdiction.
Anyway, on that assumption many years ago, and as a consequence, the Indian Act was passed, an administrative structure was created and special policies were developed for this particular ethnic group. Further, the federal government became involved in the provision of a complex set of services for Indians which other Canadians receive from provincial and local governments.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
The basic source for defining the policy of the federal government has been the Indian Act. As hon. members know, it is a comprehensive act which defines who shall be considered an Indian and how one can give up
[Mr. Andras.l

Indian status. In so doing, it establishes a special legal category defining certain rights and imposing certain restrictions. It contains provisions1 dealing with the reserve system, a system of local government, and special sections relating to taxation, liquor, inheritance and education. Although the federal administrative structure, the department of Indian affairs, stems from the Indian Act, a growing number of important departmental programs are marginal or peripheral to the Indian Act: welfare, health, community development, economic development, manpower programs etc.
This has been referred to before as well today, and I will bring it up again. The fact is that the treaties signed with Indians add another dimension to Indian-government relations. Almost all Indians express strong resentment at the failure of the government to honour and fulfill treaty and other obligations and promises. The most important of these pertain to hunting, fishing and trapping, and to the provision of land.
Hon. members have made reference today to the fact that most social and economic indicators show that the majority of Indians live in sub-marginal conditions and that relative to the rest of the population the gap in income levels, health care, educational achievements and occupational skills, while improving, is actually growing wider between the Indians and the non-Indian society. There is a significant factor explaining poverty among native peoples in Indian communities, and that is their geographical dispersion and, in many cases, the remoteness of native communities. In addition, their limited mobility has contributed to making employment and participation in the economy difficult. As a consequence, Indians have been isolated and excluded from the larger society, and the exercise of their basic human rights is seriously restricted.
We have to recognize also that cultural barriers and the insensitivity of the non-Indian society to the heritage and values of Indian life have played and continue to play a major role in excluding native peoples from the mainstream of Canadian life.

Mr. Speaker, through you I would like to thank the hon. members for their courtesy in letting me go over my time. I was wound up, and I had no idea the clock was moving that quickly.
I was commenting on the fact that I think we also have to take into consideration, in the evolution of the new policy, the fact that there is an insensitivity of the non-Indian society to the values of Indian life and that this has been a factor in excluding Indians from the mainstream. These barriers are most easily observed at two crucial points. If they could be overcome we could go a long way to correcting the situation.
These two points are where Indians come into contact with our industrial society, in educational institutions and in the labour market. Many native students enter the school system with obviously different cultural orientations and often limited or no knowledge of English or French. The educational process, one of the major instruments of socialization in any society, proves to be for the majority of Indians a maladaptive experience. In terms of getting a job, in many ways the traditional Indian way of life has not prepared the individual for occupational roles in the Canadian labour market. The new demands that they have to face-and so often they face them with a lack of understanding on the part of the people with whom they are mixing-are hard to adapt to and frequently force the Indian person into accepting sporadic, low skill employment instead of a career oriented occupational role.
Alleged Denial of Rights of Native Indians
I believe, and I know my colleague joins me, that in the past Indians have not been adequately consulted nor has their point of view been sufficiently considered in the formulation of policy and the application of programs affecting their lives. Regardless of the type of program, such paternalism and noninvolvement only encourages apathy and reduces the effectiveness of any measure because there is a resulting lack of acceptance.
This is a brief expose of the tangled web of jurisdictions, constitutional problems and contradictory objectives. That web must be untangled. I doubt there is any one single group of actions that will provide instant solutions to the deep social problem that we face with regard to our native people. However, one fact is clear. There must be change, and change there will be. Again I congratulate the hon. member for Skeena and I agree with him that in order to provide meaningful change we must go back to the basic assumptions.
The alternatives'-and I just throw these out without commitment because, as hon. members know, we are not in a position to delineate or define our policy-will obviously range from a tremendous increase in the existing structure with more budget applied to it and more people to do more of those kind of things on the one hand, to an alternative similar to the one implied by the hon. member for Skeena, or perhaps some alternatives in between these two. But whatever decision is made as to the basic objective, we must be very careful in analysing, and seeing with all the wisdom that we possess, the consequences that will flow once we have identified the objective we want to pursue. Whatever that solution will be, it must take into account the fact of the poverty among the Indian people. It must given consideration to treaties and rights and the views and attitudes of Indians toward treaties and rights. It must take into consideration and counteract the deeply rooted alienation that exists among the Indian people.
The other point which we must take into account and which has been mentioned by many hon. members is that because of the diversity of opinions and diversity of problems-which incidentally are similar to those found in almost any comparable sized group in Canada, whatever their origin or their racial background-we must be very flexible in our solutions. I do not think we can have one single approach to this.

Alleged Denial of Rights of Native Indians
In conclusion, let me say with all the conviction I can that whatever the solution may be it cannot be unilaterally imposed upon the Indian people. We must take every precaution to ensure that there is consultation and joint effort of the Indian people and the governmental people, whatever level of government is involved. There must be consultation every step of the way. We are fortunate now, as perhaps we would never have been five, ten or fifteen years ago, to recognize that there is great Indian leadership emerging in the Indian community. It is coming from the youth, but all the Indian people are awakening, and through consultation, through their own efforts, through conversations, they are becoming aware of the disparities between their lives and those of the rest of Canadian society. And they want to do something about them. We do have time to make meaningful changes and move along with them. I am encouraged by this debate to feel that this approach will be a non-partisan approach and I think, this, plus all the actions which have been taken by government, will yield solutions which will at least start us along the right path.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)

I think the step taken by the house a few minutes ago in extending this debate is a measure of the concern which is felt about this subject by members in all parts of the house. I am pleased that the debate was extended in order to provide further opportunity for discussion of this important matter.
I wish to say also that I listened with great interest to the Minister without Portfolio, the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Andras). I think he demonstrated an understanding in depth of the problems with which we are grappling in this area. I express the hope tonight that the understanding he demonstrated will be translated into legislative action and government programs and also that these will be followed by adequate implementation. Certainly, such measures will have the full support of members in this quarter of the house.
I think there is no denying that in the past there has been a significant shortfall as between plans and programs with respect to Indians and the achievements which have resulted from them. The same applies to programs and plans with respect to our Eskimo population. I could go into a lengthy analysis of this aspect, but whatever the reasons I


think this failure must also be taken into account when we are considering future programs and policies. It is a sad thing for Canadians that this house should find itself today in a position where the social and economic situation of a group of people identified by their race has deteriorated to the point at which some hon. members have found it necessary to draw special attention to it by way of the motion now before us. It is a fact that the situation of the Indian people in Canada today is a national disgrace. The problems faced by Indians were underlined forcibly by the Economic Council in its most recent annual report. As set out on page 121 the Council stated:
No discussion of poverty in Canada can avoid making special reference to the Indian, Eskimo and Metis members of our society. A few simple statistics tell a brutal story. One is that the average life expectancy of an Indian woman in Canada is 25 years. Another is that the infant mortality rate among Eskimos is about 293 deaths per thousand live births, more than ten times the infant death rate for the population as a whole.
These are not my figures; these are the figures of the Economic Council of Canada which is certainly a reputable organization with the necessary technical skills to produce accurate figures.
I might also draw attention to what is contained in a brief prepared for submission to the national Indian advisory board some three years ago. This is a statement by the Indian affairs branch submitted to the federal-provincial conference on poverty. It dealt with the health of the Indian people and we find that the average age at death of Indian males in 1963 was 33.31 years, and of Indian females, 34.71 years. The document goes on to tell us that the national average ages at death in 1963 were 60.5 for males and 64.1 for females. I might also draw attention to the summary of conclusions reached by the Economic Council, because I think these words are worth putting on record. The council recognized it did not have full capability to cover this field completely through its own operations but, it drew on the experience of many organizations which have given much study to this question.
On this basis, the council came to some conclusions to be drawn in connection with the problems we have been discussing tonight. The Economic Council's report reads, on page 123:
(1)	Indians and Eskimos are treated too much as a special group in ways which exclude them from many of the ordinary provisions of public policy-

(2)	Particular efforts will be required to help those Indians, Eskimos, and Metis who are striving to integrate themselves into the larger society-
(3)	A third major area of consensus is the need for a "community development" approach to the problems of education, individual development, adaptation to the larger environment, and community organization-*
(4)	It is clear that however much can be done to develop economic activity on reservations and in other places where significant groups of native peoples live, a continuing substantial migration to urban areas must be expected, notably in Western Canada-
(5)	It would also appear useful to initiate an immediate study of federal and provincial legislation and administration practices affecting native peoples.
As has been noted, the standard of debate has been high. We must compliment the hon. member for Skeena for his part in it. He is a recognized authority on matters we have been discussing tonight. I think, nevertheless, it is clear that a common dialogue is developing on this matter. We have had fine speeches this afternoon and this evening but, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orli-kow) said, we need action, not words. We must be careful to define what we mean by action. It is not just a case of spending money or of invoking special programs for this group. It is not just doing things for our Indian, Eskimo and Metis peoples. Our actions involve an intricate, subtle and highly complex process of interaction and development. The federal government is the agency on the spot, holding the ball. In developing its policies it must take into account the history of the conflict of white and Indian peoples, the history of the established branch of government dealing with Indians; its traditions, patterns of operation and so on, as well as the fact that there is segregation in many parts of Canada. The Government must also consider the many economic and social changes taking place in our society.
We cannot blame the federal government as such for our past history in this regard. It is a millstone which must be borne by all in Canada. The federal government has a basic constitutional responsibility to deal with these problems and, in reality, the provinces must also enter the picture.
Why did the hon. member for Skeena introduce the motion before the house, Mr. Speaker? The purpose is not to go over past history. We need to figure out where we are going. We must formulate policies that will lead to advances in this field. We need to avoid the fallacy of just measuring advances on their own merits. It is not a question of whether more people are receiving specified
DEBATES	6325
Alleged Denial of Rights of Native Indians levels of education. The question is whether these advances are keeping pace with the change in times. The problem does not involve money alone. A great deal of money is being spent, and is bringing about great improvements in certain aspects of our population. The question we must ask ourselves is, are we doing an adequate job. Are we serving the short run and long run aspirations of our Indian peoples?
Obviously, many members of the department concerned are competent, dedicated, and are trying to do a good job. But they operate within an institutional framework which stifles any efforts towards fundamental change. The motion has been brought before the house because many of us feel disturbed about what has been happening during the past year. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and other members of his party raised the expectation of our Indians when they said the Indian Act would be reviewed and that consultations might take place. Preparations for these consultations were undertaken and a booklet containing 34 questions was prepared. Incidentally, I believe all these questions were prepared for the department by the Indian Advisory Board. As I understand the situation, this is true. All the questions which were placed before the consultation meetings did originate with the particular body, but I would like to know if all the questions requested by the Indian advisory group were included. My information is that they were not, and that some of the exclusions made a significant difference. The approach to these questions was disturbing because it involved a detailed examination. The approach involved simply making revisions and slight changes to the status quo. Consultations were held with varying degrees of success. I want to commend the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Andras) for his effective and very hard work in this regard. He assured the Indian people no changes would be made in matters affecting them without adequate consultations. I fully believe the minister said this in good faith.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
Late last fall the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) announced an administrative reorganization. It became obvious there had been no consultation. Protests were made by representatives of Indian organizations. The Minister without Portfolio was put on the spot. He made some rather strong public statements regarding the government and what had happened. I will not at this point say whether he used the best
March 6. 1969
6326	COMMONS
Alleged Denial of Rights of Native Indians possible judgment with regard to the specific words he used, but nevertheless the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development replied once more that these were only administrative changes. It became obvious from sources such as the press that the minister was called on the carpet. Eventually, there was an announcement that the lines of authority were clear, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development was in charge and would be the one to decide what changes would be made to the Indian Act.
I suggest this was more than an administrative change announced by the minister. It involved community development programs. There was a reshuffling of the administrative structure. As pointed out by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) previous to that the Indian-Eskimo Association had requested that community development programs be turned over to Indian people and Indian organizations. This is a policy matter and would be a fundamental break with the past. There are responsible Indian organizations in Canada today, with capable leaders, who have a rapidly developing capacity. I suggest the first step which should be taken should be to give these organizations the opportunity to manage programs of this sort and to make decisions on these programs. The fundamental principle involved is that of selfdetermination. With respect to the Indian Act, there is a possible question of semantics involved.
There is no suggestion that treaty, legal and moral obligations made by Canada in the past must be honoured. This must be provided in the legislative framework, under whatever name the particular legislative measure might assume. A fundamental change in approach is needed and the paternalism evident in the past must be dropped. There appears to be more support for this view in all corners of this house. We need to make sure that self-determination is made possible for people of Indian ancestry. This could lead to various patterns in programs and activity. It does not mean that all Indian people will lead the same sort of lives. Involved with this principle of self-determination is the fact that people can live the type of lives they want. This is a fundamental principle to recognize. Furthermore, we need to remove the legal disabilities under which Indian people have to live at the present time.
The fundamental points we have to keep in mind are, first, it must be recognized that Indian people have the right of self-determination. The implications of this principle are


that not only does it give Indian people the full right of integration into the community and society as we know it, but also that it gives them the right to live as they wish to live. The right to make their own decision must be recognized.
Second, we must recognize commitments made by Canada as a nation to Indian people. This involves full recognition of commitments regarding land, health and other services. These rights need to be honoured as long as the Indian people collectively or individually wish to retain them.
Third, we need to get away from the centralized control of administration which has for too long featured our Indian affairs programs. Many hon. members will be aware of some of the incredible stories involved in the centralized control and bureaucracy which Indian people encounter at every turn and in almost every day of their lives.
Fourth, we need to ensure that there is integration with the community at large. For too long and under too many jurisdictions, the basic approach has been one of having special programs designed for Indian and Eskimo people. In some instances this cannot be changed overnight, but certainly we do need to adopt a fundamentally new approach.
In my own province of Saskatchewan, there are some 40,000 people of Indian ancestry who are regarded as treaty Indians. There are nearly 40,000 others of mixed ancestry, some of them referred to as Indian people and some as Metis people. There are eight Indian reserves in my own constituency, and a large number of Indians living in the city of Kegina. In the past, they lived largely on
In some parts of the province there are still treaty obligations which have not been honoured. In southern Saskatchwam the reserves are largely on agricultural land. The people have lived in a basically rural atmosphere which provided a fairly stable form of existence for some years. The economic instability of the 1930's and the 1940's the political instability and in fact some of the social upheavals of this' period, produced great changes. From that time on it became increasingly difficult for people of Indian ancestry to cope with the problems they encountered.
On our reserves we have agricultural land that has not been developed. I can cite many instances and examples where this could be considered to be solely due to the smothering paternalism that has been a feature of public policy in the past. Much of this land is rented
March 6, 1969

out to people off the reserves who have made arrangements with the Indian affairs branch, and with very little consultation with the Indian people themselves. They are the ones who are now using this land.
It is true that some development projects have been carried out. There are a couple of projects in my own constituency at the present time involving community pastures on the Muskowekwan and Gordon Indian reserves. I have some details which I obtained from the government on this matter and I find that Indian people do not have the necessary resources to make full use of this pasture at the present time. Indians will be given first claim to the use of this pasture, but the answer to my question also stated that Indians do not now have sufficient cattle to fully stock the pastures and so the remaining capacity will be made available to people of non-Indian ancestry. What will happen to Indian people when they do wish and are able to make use of these community pastures? These facilities will then be used under contractual arrangements made with people outside the Indian reserve. It is also clear that these pastures will be managed by other than Indian people. They will be managed by government departments and agencies. Again, I say this is the type of thing that is still going on for which there is no need. This is another reason we felt we had to bring this motion before the house.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
In conclusion, therefore, I suggest that we do need fundamental changes in our approach to the Indian Act. A meaningful program involving a new approach of self-determination for the Indian people should be started now. Tonight we are not dealing with personalities, but we are dealing with the welfare of people.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in the debate this evening. I should like to express my appreciation to the members of the house for extending the sitting. I am sure members will excuse me if I do not make any preliminary remarks because I should like to raise one particular issue. I know there are other speakers who wish to follow. Before I get into that issue, however, I should like to say I believe what the Indian people are saying to us today is that in their view the basic policy objective must be full and equal citizenship. There are many obstacles in the path to that objective. The one to which I should like to draw the attention of the members this evening has already been mentioned. It is the role of the provinces in assisting Indians to lead contemporary lives as Canadian citizens.
I think one of the most serious obstacles of all to a contemporary life for Indians is our misconception of the role of the province; that is, it is commonly thought Indians are the sole responsibility of the federal government. This misconception of the direct role and responsibility of the province is shown by governments themselves, by most Indian people and by the general public. It results in a special intense relationship of the Indian people with the federal government and a severely attenuated relationship with the provinces. This I think is an indefensible and discriminatory arrangement which denies equality, is a bar to integration and, I believe, is without foundation in the constitution. It results from historical reasons and is reinforced by current political pressures on the federal government to do more. The more Ottawa does-and I am one of those who thinks it should do a great deal more-the more it tends to lock Indian citizens into an unequal and separate existence.
My argument is that this unacceptable division of federal-provincial functions is neither required nor justified by the constitution or by Indian treaties. It should neither be tolerated by Indians nor by the general public. A more complete statement of the legal basis of the argument than I can give can be found in the Hawthorn-Tremblay report of 1960 and particularly the writings of Dr. Kenneth Lysyk of the Faculty of Law of the University of British Columbia. When one looks at the constitution one finds there is no doubt at all
March 6. 1969
6328	COMMONS
Alleged Denial of Rights of Native Indians that under the British North America Act, section 91 paragraph 24, it is the federal parliament that has the exclusive authority to legislate for Indians and lands reserved for Indians. It should be noted that this section does not read "Indians on lands reserved for Indians" but by its wording indicates that parliament may legislate for Indians whether reserve based or not, as well as for lands reserved for Indians.
I want to discuss in the short time available Indians only, since Indian lands are in a different and special category, being singled out in a way that health, education and other matters are not singled out. It has been forcefully argued, and I think correctly, that whereas the provinces cannot legislate specifically for Indians as such, there is nothing in the constitution that says that provincial laws of general application-for example, in the field of health which is normally a provincial responsibility-should not apply to Indian persons as to all other provincial residents. It is only that kind of legislation that is clearly for Indians that is reserved to Ottawa. When the federal parliament legislates specifically for Indians, it can and does intrude on fields normally reserved for the provinces, though at the expense of perpetuating a specialized monopoly of services to a separated class of Canadians identified on ethnic and cultural grounds.
Even in this latter case, when the federal government does legislate it is not mandatory for it to do so; it is simply permissive for it to legislate in order to implement federal policies in Indian affairs. The Indian Act and its regulations is such a piece of federal legislation which only the federal government can pass under the constitution, since it is directed specifically and only to Indians as defined under the act. A province could not pass an Indian Act, but the general laws of a province and its programs and policies can none the less apply to Indians in the province within limits.
Therefore, I think it is important to question where those limits lie and how flexible and responsive they can be to Indian needs. It is important to an Indian future for Indians to determine to what extent it would be in their interest to alter the federal-provincial balance or to mix it. This federal-provincial balance may be altered, for example, more in the direction of the province, as is happening in several provinces under Indian pressure, such as Saskatchewan and Manitoba.


Some significant flexibility does appear available so far as the constitution is concerned, except in respect of Indian lands. This is an exclusive federal responsibility. Firm limitations on provincial legislative competence do exist, however, in two sources other than in the constitution. These are found in the treaties and the Indian Act. An example of the conflict of provincial law with treaty provisions is found in the fact that the provincial game laws do not apply. Nor are provincial laws applicable if they conflict with the Indian Act or its regulations; that is, whenever the federal parliament has already occupied a given field with Indian legislation.
These limitations on provincial competence are thus significant, but they relate largely to the extent to which the federal government has already occupied a field which might already be under provincial jurisdiction by devising its own Indian policy in that field. Therefore, in many cases, except with respect to treaty provisions, the removal of some of the limitations on provincial legislative competence rests with the federal government by way of change in the Indian Act. Perhaps, therefore, new options will become available to Indians and governments as a result of current consultations with the Indians with respect to amendments to the Indian Act.
When a consensus is reached on changes in the act, it may well be-and I suspect this will be the case-that substantially greater automomy will devolve upon Indian band governments. They may then choose, under the less confining provisions of a revised Indian Act, to relate themselves more directly to provincial laws and services. They may gradually relinquish or modify the special services provided exclusively by the federal government.
Indians will properly ask whether a shift in federal-provincial patterns of responsibility can take place to their advantage without adversely affecting rights that they regard as theirs. I believe the answer is yes. They will ask whether the federal constitutional responsibility would thereby be reduced. I believe the answer is no; there would be no change.

At this point I would like to say two things, Mr. Speaker. I think, first, the federal government can be faulted for a failing to clarify the true constitutional position to the public and to conduct intensive discussions of the problems and options with Indians and the provinces. In the absence of consultation,
March 6. 1969

Indian communities are left vaguely uneasy about changes they find it difficult to discern. If I had had time earlier, Mr. Speaker, I would have stressed the very important role of a task force in developing a new consensus and a new policy orientation.
I would refer again to the need, as the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) or the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) reminded us this afternoon, of high level federal-provincial conferences to activate, with Indian consent, the unfulfilled responsibilities of the provinces. In addition, I think it was never more important than now to clarify Indian rights under treaties, and aboriginal rights where there are no treaties, for example with respect to hunting and fishing rights and with respect to claims to title or interest in lands. It is essential to restore rights that have been abridged, and to meet obligations that have been unfulfilled.
The time is overdue for settling outstanding claims, whether aboriginal or treaty, through either direct negotiation, which has much to commend it, through development of agreements or a claims commission, with compensation where appropriate. It seems to me, moreover, that if the consultative process is to be comprehensive, flexible and genuine, the question of how to settle past grievances and claims, including the technique of the proposed claims commission, should be part of that consultation process, since only by consultation on these methods can the claims and needs of the future be related to the claims of the past. Only in this way, I think, can a developmental momentum be generated and maintained.
Consultation concerning treaty rights should be part of the discussions concerning the role of the provinces, and both should be part of the consultations concerning development programs for a new future. I am stressing that the consultation process must be comprehensive if all of the options open to Indians1 and government are to be usefully examined.
I think it is fair to conclude that the federal government, with Indian consent, has considerable freedom to determine the kind and scope of responsibilities it will assume under the grant of constitutional power in section 91 of the British North America Act and under the resulting Indian Act. It is evident, I think, that only if the provinces, under Indian and public pressures, change their attitude and expand their legitimate functions will it be possible to talk of successful participation
Alleged Denial of Rights of Native Indians by Indian citizens in contemporary Canadian life at all levels.
Reserve communities should not remain federal islands within provincial boundaries, frustrating a people in search of equality through development. If and when a province extends its general programs and services to Indian residents, whether on or off reserves, it does not assume a responsibility that constitutionally belongs to another government and consequently should not be paid for doing so. It is simply fulfilling its own responsibilities. No doubt a case can be made for cost-sharing on historical grounds or grounds other than constitutional.
It seems possible to resolve the question of a more federal-provincial mix of functions and services on utilitarian grounds, because treaty and constitutional barriers are slight. The particular mix in any given case at any given time is a matter of policy and agreement, not a matter of the constitution. The choice in altering the governmental balance lies largely with the Indian people.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank hon. members here for agreeing to extend this sitting tonight so that those of us who wanted to say something about the Indian people of Canada would have the opportunity of doing so.
At the outset, I would like to say something about the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) and the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Andras). I think that as a result of the approach of both these ministers to Indian affairs, to consultation with the Indian people of Canada and to the relationship between the Indian people and the government of Canada, we have entered a new era in this field. I believe that both these ministers have taken upon themselves a heavy responsibility, as we realized today when we listened to members on all sides of this house, each with his own idea, his own theories and his own approach to this very perplexing matter and to how it should be resolved within our confederation. I think both these ministers have shown a great deal of courage, a number of new ideas and a lot of strength.
Having followed the discussions in this chamber today, as a member of parliament I have the feeling that those of us who sit in the House of Commons as Canadians, many of us representing the Indian people, are, like many other Canadians, concerned about our first citizens. But I think that with a little
March 6, 1969
6330	COMMONS
Alleged Denial of Rights of Native Indians fear and trepidation, many of us ask ourselves whether or not we are able to offer much that is constructive. I listened with bewilderment to some of the suggested solutions to our problems with respect to the Indians. We can look back to our history and see that all has not been well and that many of the policies adopted have been based on a concept that is not acceptable in today's society. I could not help but feel again today that we who represent many people offer solutions which are not really solutions which the Indian people themselves want. I listened with a great deal of interest to the hon. member for Coast-Chilcotin (Mr. St. Pierre) who said that there is not just one solution, there are many.
I listened to others who suggested that in their own areas there were particular problems which were not necessarily part of a national problem. May I suggest for a moment that one of the things that we have to do as legislators in Canada is to recognize that we cannot offer the solutions, that we must look to the Indian people themselves to come up with their own ideas and thoughts, and that it is not an easy thing for us to be able to do this. I think that if we suggest for one minute that the Indian Act is not something that we can amend, we will look like people who know not what they say. For example, I think of the problems of treaties No. 8 and 11 in the north on which the Indian people have many ideas. I think also of the concern that people have about the treaties which were signed by their forefathers only 45 or 47 years ago, and whether they have had any real effect on their lives.
[DOT] (10:40 p.m.)
The fact that the federal authority has not implemented certain aspects of these treaties has I believe destroyed some of the faith which the Indian people have in the great white father. In this process of communicating with the Indian people and establishing good faith I believe it is incumbent on us as politicians to identify these problems positively. But in the name of Heaven let us not use them for the sake of political advantage. I cannot but be concerned when I listen to continued attacks on a particular administration. I am thinking in terms of the Akaitcho Hall affair which the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) has raised in this house on several occasions. I respect the hon. member for having brought this up in the first instance but I am not persuaded he should continue to play on it when those of us who are acquainted with this situation know there


are forces at work within the community to change it. Let us take this kind of situation out of the public domain. Let us not play on the feelings of the Indian people or of the Eskimo people or of the Metis people or of any other group.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Leader of the N.D.P.
speechtext: How would you change things, then?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
I have lived in Yellowknife, the location of this institution. Maybe all is not well. As I said, I respect the hon. member for having brought this matter to the attention of the house, but I believe the administration of the hostel felt they could handle the situation once it had been brought out into the open.
In line with what I was saying a minute ago, I do not wish to pursue this subject. There are other areas going beyond the Indian Act and an Indian claims commission where a dialogue could be established with the Indian people. We could help achieve this by doing things, by building homes, educating the young people and developing the economic potential of the reserves, something which is extremely important. I believe the minister is aware of this. I believe he wants to do these things. I suggest to him, to the department and to this house that with the continuing goodwill shown by this assembly toward the Indian people of Canada we can accomplish something realistic, beyond partisan considerations, beyond the politics with which many of us are so familiar.
There are many other things which I am sure all of us would like to say. One area which is most important in terms of the goodwill which must be established between the Indian people and the other people of Canada involves enforcement of the Migratory Birds Convention. The Indian people, in accordance with their treaties, believed in their hearts and minds that they had the right to hunt and shoot the animals and birds of the land and the sky. They felt they had this right for as long as the sun rises in the east and sets in the west-they thought of it in such terms. I know there are many who would say that the Migratory Birds Convention should not be amended because to do so would not be in the interests of conservation. I suggest to the minister that shooting the few additional birds which otherwise might not be shot will have little effect on the bird population of this country. I also believe that if the Indian people of this country are given responsibility
March 6, 1969	COMMONS
in this field and authority to shoot those birds they feel it is necessary to shoot, they will prove fully responsible and will behave as we expect them to.
It has been suggested that we should abolish the department of Indian affairs, take the money now spent on the department and use it to improve the living standards of Indian families. I suggest instead that we should examine how much it costs to educate our young Indian people. As Canadians we all want our Indian people to take their full part in our Canadian way of life.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I understand there is a gentleman's agreement for two hon. members to share the last ten minutes available. On that basis, I think it would be fair to all hon. members if I were to recognize at this time the hon. member for York South.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Leader of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall leave most of the remaining time to the other hon. member who wishes to speak. I wish to make three brief statements.
I make no apology for having continued to pursue the Akaitcho Hall incident. I would not have done so if the minister, on the first occasion I raised the question, had said, "I know about it; it is wrong and I intend to correct it." He did not say that but spoke of other matters with which I will not deal. In such situations, the only way to bring about change is by having the courage of one's convictions and by continuing to insist that the change ought to take place. That is the only way we shall bring about changes to this act.
Secondly, we introduced this general subject because, in the view of our party and many members of the house, the sort of discussion that has take nplace today was long overdue. It was necessary to obtain from the minister the kinds of statements we have heard from him. Having introduced the motion, the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) set a high level of debate. He introduced debate at that high level precisely because we wanted an earnest discussion of the issues involved. We did not want, as the hon. member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Orange) has suggested in connection with the question of Akaitcho Hall, to make this merely a political debate. It was nothing of the sort.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I say on behalf of my colleagues that I do not blame the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development 29180-401
DEBATES	6331
Alleged Denial of Rights of Native Indians (Mr. Chretien) and the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Andras) for not being very specific about policies they are not yet ready to enunciate. I say to them on behalf of my colleagues and, I am sure, on behalf of all members of the house, that we heard with interest and anticipation their statements that they intend to end the era of paternalism; that they intend to recognize the basic human rights involved in this issue; and that they intend to listen to our Indians and pursue policies that will embody the wishes of those people. This is what they said and we shall hold them to their statements.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Leader of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
I hope the legislation they will bring down in a few weeks, not in a few years, will fulfil in toto those promises to the Indian people of this country. I hope it will recognize their right and really enable them to integrate themselves into our society as Canadians. On behalf of my colleagues I say to the minister and the government, we will accept nothing less when the legislation comes.
[DOT] (10:50 p.m.)

The trip to the Northwest Territories and Yukon taken by members of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development at the end of January this year allowed us to visit five Indian and one Eskimo communities. The trip was taken at the end of January so that members could experience northern living conditions during the Arctic winter season.
Among the objectives was a look at northern housing and employment conditons, particularly as they affected Indian and Eskimo peoples. We were exposed to a representative cross-section of the problems which affect our Indian people across Canada by visiting those two communities.
Some of the housing conditions we encountered at Copper-mine on the shores of the Bering Sea were much better than I expected. Almost all the residents of this village live in homes built during the past three or four years. On the other hand, some of the worst housing I have seen anywhere was on the outskirts of Whitehorse in a slum area inhabited by whites and Indians. This slum section, referred to locally as Sleepy Hollow, is much worse than the local Indian village.
The physical progress in the north in the form of new housing and new school facilities is encouraging. I travelled across the north in

6332	COMMONS
Alleged Denial of Rights of Native Indians 1966 as a member of the House of Commons Standing Committee on Northern Affairs. This physical progress was undeniably obvious. There was a hopeful sign in the attitude of people in the local communities toward the problems of their fellow citizens of Indian origin. In 1966, it appeared to me that the white communities were interested only in their own problems. In 1969, there were signs of genuine interest on the part of the average white northerner in helping native people to full participation within the modern economy which is developing so rapidly in these northern communities.
I have spoken so far of progress and hope, but that is far from the whole story in the north. Last autumn the standing committee studied the employment situation of our native Indian and Eskimo people and found it to be generally deplorable. The unemployment rate for employable adult Indian males is in the 40 per cent to 50 per cent range. For a portion of the year at least that percentage of adult Indian males is unemployed. This was confirmed by our visit to the north. Coppermine appears to be a prosperous community, yet almost the entire male population was unemployed at the time of our visit.
Even though mining exploration was in progress last summer in the Coppermine River area, only 40 or 59 miles away, very few of the local residents were employed on those projects. Something is radically wrong with a system when southern labour must be brought from thousands of miles away to work in an area that has a native labour surplus. We had public meetings at each place which we visited. At our public meeting in Coppermine we asked the young men present how many of them would be interested in working on mine drilling rigs and we got a substantial response. We found out that within the last six months to a year the department instituted a number of new programs which will quickly lead to a great many more of our young Indian and Eskimo people being trained for positions in northern based industry.

In 1965 I wrote a letter to the then minister of northern affairs in which I suggested that one method to absorb more of our native northern people into the labour force would be to convene a conference of representatives of northern based industry, northern based labour unions and other parties, including representatives of provincial departments of labour, the federal department of indian affairs and, of course, representatives of the Indian people themselves.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I don't think we have a quorum in the house at the present time on this important question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the hon. member calling for a count?

Yes, sir, I am.
And the count being made, more that 20 members were declared to be present.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Surrey (Mr. Mather) is in error. There is a quorum.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to take another minute to complete my remarks. I urge the minister to consider again convening a conference of people with experience in this field to attack this labour problem. I also give notice, as chairman of the committee, that we intend to call before the committee representatives of northern based industry that is not employing sufficient numbers of native people, and representatives of northern based labour unions that are not contributing sufficiently to the employment of native personnel in the north.

speechtext:
As it is now past ten o'clock, I must inform the house that pursuant to standing order 58 (11) this debate is deemed to be closed.
Accordingly, the house stands adjourned until eleven o'clock to-morrow morning.
